bio.en: Andrew Wilkinson is co-founder and CEO of Tiny, a holding company often called the Berkshire Hathaway of the internet that owns over 40 businesses, and has started and run more companies than almost anyone.
bio.zh: Andrew Wilkinson 是 Tiny 的联合创始人兼 CEO，这家控股公司常被称为“互联网界的伯克希尔·哈撒韦”，旗下拥有 40 多家企业，他创办并运营过的公司数量几乎无人能及。

summary.en: Andrew shares strategies for coming up with a great business idea—advising first-time founders not to swing for the fences immediately and to “fish where the fish are” rather than enter repeatedly failed business models. He describes AI as a tireless $200-a-month employee that will massively change knowledge work, and grapples with whether all jobs eventually become a single prompt. The conversation also covers what he's learned about happiness, money, and building durable businesses.
summary.zh: Andrew 分享了想出优秀商业点子的策略——建议首次创业者不要一开始就全力冲刺，要“到有鱼的地方钓鱼”，而非进入那些反复失败的模式。他把 AI 形容为每月 200 美元、永不疲倦的员工，将极大改变知识工作，并思考所有工作是否最终都变成一句提示词。对话还涵盖他在幸福、金钱和打造持久业务方面的心得。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: You don't want to walk into the gym on day one and try and deadlift 300 pounds. So when someone comes to me and they're a first time entrepreneur and they say, "I'm going to make the next great AI company," I think that is the equivalent.
turns.zh: 你不会第一天进健身房就想硬拉 300 磅。所以当有人来找我，是个第一次创业的人，说'我要做下一个伟大的 AI 公司'，我觉得这就相当于那种事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like you've actually started and run more companies than maybe anyone else in the world. What is your best advice for coming up with a great startup idea?
turns.zh: 我感觉你创办和运营过的公司可能比世界上任何人都要多。关于想出一个好的创业点子，你最好的建议是什么？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's longtime business partner, has this amazing quote.
turns.zh: Charlie Munger，Warren Buffett 多年的合伙人，有一句很棒的话。

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.en: Fish where the fish are.
turns.zh: 到有鱼的地方钓鱼。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: The biggest mistakes I've made have been going into business models where other people have repeatedly failed and thinking, I can do this better.
turns.zh: 我犯过的最大错误，就是进入那些别人已经反复失败过的商业模式，然后心里想着'我能做得更好'。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so funny to watch you on Twitter. Clearly you've become AI obsessed.
turns.zh: 看你在 Twitter 上的样子真好笑。显然你已经变成了 AI 痴迷者。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: It's like having the world's most reliable employee who costs $200 a month and works 24/7. So many knowledge work jobs are going to change massively. I think the fundamental question is, do all jobs just become a single prompt?
turns.zh: 这就像拥有一个世界上最可靠的员工，每月只要 200 美元，而且 24/7 全天候工作。很多知识工作都会发生巨变。我觉得最根本的问题是：所有工作最终会不会都变成一句提示词？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've been wanting to chat with you for so long. turns.zh: 我一直想跟你聊很久了。有太多我想聊的，我想从一个我知道你思考很多、也是很多人心里都在想的话题开始，就是想出一个好的创业点子。现在很多人都在想这件事，因为 AI 让把你的点子变成真实的东西变得很容易，我觉得这是你花了很多时间思考的事情。我感觉你创办和运营过的公司比——我不知道，可能比世界上任何人都要多。我觉得你能排进前一百、前十之类的。我说不准，这感觉对吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: I've definitely had a lot of experiences and I've probably started or been involved with 75 different projects or businesses where I've been a primary contributor and I wouldn't say that's anything to brag about because I've been an inch deep in a mile wide. So that's been in a lot of ways kind of my Achilles heel is I get too excited about ideas and I start too many businesses, but as a result I've seen almost every business model under the sun.
turns.zh: 我确实有很多经历，我大概创办过或参与过 75 个不同的项目或公司，都是我作为主要贡献者的。我不觉得这有什么好吹的，因为我是'一英里宽、一英寸深'。所以在很多方面这其实是我阿喀琉斯之踵——我太容易对点子兴奋，开了太多公司——但结果就是我几乎见过天底下所有的商业模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. Yeah, I think the benefit is for us is we get to learn from your experience. Let me just ask you this question, what is your best advice for coming up with a great startup idea?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。是啊，我觉得对我们来说好处就是可以从你的经验中学习。我就直接问你这个问题吧：关于想出一个好的创业点子，你最好的建议是什么？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Ultimately the best thing is something you're going to be interested in, but I think a mistake a lot of people make is they choose something that everybody is interested in. So for example, they say I don't know anyone that has hadn't had the thought, man, I would love to start a really cool restaurant or I want to have a cool cafe or something. And in reality, what they think about is how cool would it be to come up with an amazing logo or all fun stuff, design the menu and stuff. But in reality, operating those businesses is miserable and it's also a very hard business because every morning millions of people wake up and they go, I should start a cafe. But on the flip side, almost nobody wakes up every morning and says, "You know what? I'd love to start a funeral home," or "I would like to start a pest control business," or "I should start software that helps people fill out forms for the government." (00:06:26): And Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's longtime business partner, has this amazing quote. He says, "Fish where the fish are." And he gives this example, he says, "If you're a fisherman and you see a large pond and all around the pond, there's a whole bunch of fishermen and they're all elbowing each other out of the way. They're all using the best lures, the best fishing line, they all have amazing strategy. You actually want to walk off into the forest and find a small fishing hole with lots of fish and very little competition. And I think that's probably the most important thing in business is actually to find those niches where you can actually make real money because competition equals lower margin. The more competitors there are, the lower your prices have to be and the more competitive the business is ultimately.
turns.zh: 归根结底，最好的事情是你会有兴趣去做的事，但我觉得很多人犯的一个错误是，他们选择了一个所有人都感兴趣的东西。比如，他们说——我不认识谁没动过这个念头——'哎，我想开一家很酷的餐厅'或者'我想开个很酷的咖啡馆'之类的。而实际上，他们脑子里想的是'设计一个超棒的 logo 多酷啊'，还有那些好玩的事、设计菜单之类的。但实际上，运营这些生意是很痛苦的，而且也是一门很难的生意，因为每天早上都有几百万人醒来然后说'我应该开个咖啡馆'。但反过来，几乎没有人每天早上醒来会说'你知道吗，我想开一家殡仪馆'或者'我想开一家害虫防治公司'或者'我应该做一个帮人填政府表格的软件'。(00:06:26)：Charlie Munger，Warren Buffett 多年的合伙人，有一句很棒的话。他说：'到有鱼的地方钓鱼。'他举了这个例子，他说：'如果你是个渔夫，你看到一个大池塘，池塘周围有一大堆渔夫，他们都在互相挤来挤去，都在用最好的鱼饵、最好的鱼线，都有超棒的策略。你其实应该走进森林，找一个有很多鱼但竞争很少的小钓鱼洞。'我觉得这可能是商业中最重要的——就是找到那些你真正能赚到钱的利基市场，因为竞争等于更低的利润率。竞争者越多，你的价格就得越低，生意最终就越激烈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It doesn't feel intuitive to go after small markets and to find niches. So let's just follow that thread. Well, why is that actually a source of some of the best ideas starting really small and niche?
turns.zh: 去追小市场、找利基，这感觉不太直觉。那我们就顺着这条线聊。为什么这其实是最好的点子来源之一——从很小、很利基开始？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: I don't necessarily think it has to be something that is small forever, but it has to be something that like I think about if you're a first time entrepreneur or a student or something, you don't want to walk into the gym on day one and try and deadlift 300 pounds. So when someone comes to me and they're a first time entrepreneur and they say, "I'm going to make the next great AI company," or "I'm going to launch a new bank," or something like that, something that is very, very rigorous and complicated and highly competitive and regulated, I think that is the equivalent. I think you really want to take the baby weights and start slowly building your muscle. And I think about my own experience starting a business, I was so lucky because the first business I ever started my web design agency, which became Metalab, that was so easy and it worked immediately because all I had to do was know how to build websites and be able to talk to potential customers. (00:08:33): And then once they said, "Yes, I will pay you $5,000," I just had to send them an invoice, do the work, and that was it. It was a very simple business. And because of that, I got immediate positive feedback and I built my own narrative. And my narrative was, "I'm good at business, I can do this, keep going." And then I went off and I started taking my money that I made from that original business and that's when I fucked up. So I went out and I started a pizzeria and I lost all my money. I started a designer cat furniture business, a online DJ school, a skin cream business, all of these things. I've just lost all my money almost immediately, but because I had that first win I kept on going. And I just think it's so critical that people choose a business where they get that initial win.
turns.zh: 我不一定认为它必须永远很小，但必须是一件……我想想，如果你是个第一次创业的人或者学生之类的，你不会第一天进健身房就想硬拉 300 磅。所以当有人来找我，是个第一次创业的人，说'我要做下一个伟大的 AI 公司'或者'我要开一家新银行'之类的——那种非常非常严苛、复杂、竞争激烈且受监管的事情——我觉得这就相当于那个。我觉得你真的应该从最轻的重量开始，慢慢练肌肉。我想到我自己的创业经历，我非常幸运，因为我办的第一个公司——我的网页设计代理公司，后来变成了 Metalab——非常简单，立刻就成功了，因为我只需要知道怎么做网站、能和潜在客户聊天就行。(00:08:33)：然后他们一说'好，我付你 5000 美元'，我就给他们开张发票、把活干了，就这么简单。这是一门非常简单的生意。正因为如此，我得到了即时的正向反馈，建立了自己的叙事。我的叙事是：'我擅长做生意，我能做到，继续下去。'然后我就开始把从那个原始生意里赚到的钱拿去……那是我搞砸的时候。我去开了一家披萨店，把钱全赔了。我开了设计师猫家具公司、在线 DJ 学校、护肤霜公司，所有这些东西。我几乎立刻就把钱全赔光了，但因为有了第一次胜利，我一直坚持下来了。我就是觉得，选择一门能让你获得初次胜利的生意，这太关键了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, this is a great topic. This is just like how do you avoid creating a job for yourself that you hate? There's a lot of business opportunities and ideas that like, "Yeah, you can make this work," and then it works, and then you're stuck doing this thing running a restaurant. My wife tells a story where a friend started a coffee shop and then he's like, "I thought I was starting a coffee shop, but I'm just replacing milk and buying milk all day. That's my job now." So just kind of along those lines to help people avoid creating a beast that they didn't expect any advice for Just how to know this is maybe even though this may work and make money, you probably don't want to be spending your life doing this sort of business.
turns.zh: 好，这是个很好的话题。这就像是怎么避免给自己创造一份你讨厌的工作。有很多商业机会和点子，就是'嗯，你能把这个做起来'，然后做起来了，然后你就被困在经营餐厅这种事里了。我老婆讲过一个故事，一个朋友开了家咖啡店，然后他说'我以为我开的是咖啡店，但我现在的工作就是整天换牛奶、买牛奶'。所以就着这个思路，为了帮大家避免养出一个自己没想到的怪物——有什么建议吗？就是怎么知道这门生意即使能做成、能赚钱，你大概也不应该把一辈子花在这种生意上？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: So I just started a pressure washing business. I was speaking at a local business school and after I spoke, one of the kids walked up to me and he said, "Hey, I'm an entrepreneur. I've started two or three businesses in the past doing landscaping and I'm not enjoying school." And so just on the spot, I said to him, "Why don't you drop out and we'll start a business together?" And I'd been cooking on this idea of a pressure washing business because I'd studied that industry a little bit and I knew a few friends who'd done it in other cities. And I had this unfair advantage, which is I owned a whole bunch of media properties where I could advertise it for free basically. And so we started this business and I think for him, he kind of had this moment of, do I really want to be washing people's driveways for the rest of my life? (00:10:47): And what I said to him is, "Look, if this gets to scale, you'll never touch a pressure washer unless you want to." If the business can get big enough where you can have employees, he can just focus on sales or digital marketing or whatever aspect of the business that he really loves. And I think that's the biggest thing that a lot of entrepreneurs miss. They say, "I don't want to do that for the rest of my life. I don't want to be in the back of a dry cleaner dry cleaning clothes." And to me it's just a question of scale. I think the cafe is a great example because a cafe, if it doesn't get to a reasonable scale is just a job. (00:11:26): There's a big difference between a business and a job. I think if you could start a pressure washing business where you're the only employee, yeah, that's a job, but if you can get to a scale where you can drive 10 leads a day, then you don't have to do any of the pressure washing and you just do what you love. So I think a lot of people have this kind of Protestant work ethic where they think, well, I've got to be the person to do everything. And I think they really need to lean into what I call lazy leadership, which is how do I get away from the things I hate as quickly as humanly possible? How do I be Teflon for tasks?
turns.zh: 我刚开了一家高压清洗公司。我去一所本地商学院演讲，讲完之后，有个学生走过来跟我说：'嘿，我是个创业者，我之前做过两三个生意，做园林绿化的，我不太喜欢学校。'于是我当场对他说：'你为什么不退学，我们一起开个公司？'我一直在琢磨高压清洗这个生意，因为我研究过那个行业一点，也认识几个在其他城市做过的朋友。我有一个不公平的优势，就是我拥有一大堆媒体资源，基本上可以免费打广告。于是我们就开了这家公司。我觉得对他来说，他有点那个时刻——我真的要一辈子给人洗车道吗？(00:10:47)：我跟他说的是：'你看，如果这做到规模，你再也不用碰高压清洗机，除非你想碰。'如果生意能大到可以雇人，他就可以专注于销售或数字营销或者他真正喜欢的那个部分。我觉得这是很多创业者忽略的最大的一点。他们说'我不想一辈子干这个，我不想在干洗店后面给人干洗衣服'。对我来说，这只是规模的问题。我觉得咖啡馆是个很好的例子，因为咖啡馆如果做不到合理的规模，那就只是一份工作。(00:11:26)：生意和工作有很大区别。我觉得如果你开一家高压清洗公司，你是唯一的员工，嗯，那是一份工作；但如果你能做到每天能拿到 10 个线索的规模，那你就不需要做任何高压清洗了，只做你喜欢的事就行。所以我觉得很多人有那种新教徒式的工作伦理，觉得'我得什么都自己干'。我觉得他们真的需要多依靠别人，把事情委托出去，专注于自己真正擅长和喜欢的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting that this business is non-software related at all, this pressure washing business. So I guess just for folks that are coming up with ideas, and I imagine most ideas are there's a pull to make it software oriented, something AI is going to help build for you and help you run. What's your calculus on just going down a direction of real world physical business, like a restaurant power washing business versus a software just like what are the benefits of that direction when should someone actually seriously think about doing a business like a power washing business?
turns.zh: 有意思的是这门生意跟软件完全无关，这个高压清洗的生意。所以对于想点子的人来说，我猜大多数点子——都有一种把它做成软件的拉力，做成 AI 会帮你构建和运营的东西。对于走现实世界实体生意这条路——比如餐厅、高压清洗——你的权衡是什么？走这条路有什么好处？什么时候应该认真考虑做像高压清洗这样的生意？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: I think if someone's listening to this podcast, odds are they're someone who's kind of a digital native. And I think the question is, what's your unfair advantage and what are you great at? So for me, I think I have reasonably good taste. And so what I could do is I identify and I knew enough to identify great design and development talent, but mostly I was lucky because I was a talker. I was good at meeting with clients and selling myself. And so ultimately my highest and best use my superpower was sales. And so that can be applied to anything, anything where you need to go out and you need to sell a customer. And so really it just comes down to what do you get drawn to and then how do you find the profitable business within that? So here's an example. A friend of mine, he owns a restaurant and he said, "Oh, I love it. I'm so passionate about it. It's this stunning beautiful restaurant in my hometown." (00:13:32): And he said, "But it's really just a job for a few different people and we can't make any money at it, but I've been noticing that there's all these vendors that service the restaurant and those guys are making a killing." And so he told me about a business that cleans grease traps, another one that cleans exhaust vents for kitchens. So I think looking around and seeing where your passion is and then sniffing around within it, probably somewhere within your passion, there's an opportunity. So for example, I love movies. My happy place is a dark theater. That's the best way for me to de-stress is go to a dark theater and watch a movie and get lost in it. And probably about four or five years ago, I was like, "Man, how cool would it be to invest in movies in some way to be a part of that creative world?" (00:14:26): And so I started looking into funding movies and I realized that when you fund movies, like 90% of the time you lose all your money. And even if you do make some money, you rarely make a good return. But I spend a bunch of time understanding the industry and learning about it. And then two years ago I was in New Zealand and I met the founder of Letterboxd and I realized, "Oh my God, this is a business where this has a moat, so it has a network effect, it's a huge social network for film reviewers. It's something I'm passionate about and it's something that we can buy at a fair price." All those things came together and I was like, "Oh my god, I can invest in film now." In the same way I used to be a barista, we ended up buying the AeroPress coffee maker company. So I follow my passions and spend a long time learning different industries and then I find the profitable niche within.
turns.zh: 我觉得听这个播客的人，大概率是数字原住民。问题在于：你的不公平优势是什么？你擅长什么？对我来说，我觉得我品味还不错。我能做的是——我也懂 enough 去识别优秀的设计和开发人才——但 mostly 我很幸运，因为我是个会说话的人，我擅长跟客户见面、推销自己。所以归根结底我最高最擅长的用途、我的超能力是销售。这个能力可以应用到任何事情上——任何你需要出去卖东西给客户的场景。所以其实就归结于：你被什么吸引？然后你怎么在其中找到赚钱的生意？举个例子。我有个朋友，他开了一家餐厅，他说：'哦，我爱死了，我超有热情，这是我家乡一家超美的餐厅。'(00:13:32)：他说：'但其实它只是给几个人提供了一份工作，我们赚不到钱。但我注意到有好多给餐厅做服务的供应商，那些家伙赚翻了。'他跟我讲了一家清洗油脂分离器的公司，还有一家清洗厨房排风口的。所以我觉得，看看你的热情在哪里，然后在里面到处嗅一嗅，可能你的热情范围内就有一个机会。比如我，我爱电影，我的快乐老家就是一个黑暗的电影院。那是我减压最好的方式——去一个黑暗的影院看一部电影，沉浸进去。大概四五 年前，我想：'哇，要是能投资电影多酷啊，能成为那个创意世界的一部分？'(00:14:26)：于是我开始研究投资电影，我发现投资电影 90% 的时候你会把钱全赔光，即使赚了点钱，也很少有好的回报。但我花了不少时间深挖，最终我发现电影周边产品——比如官方授权的商品、道具复刻品——才是真正赚钱的。所以我投了一家做电影周边的公司，它非常赚钱，而且让我能参与到那个创意世界。所以我觉得，在你的热情领域里到处挖一挖，通常里面会有一个赚钱的机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, and this is a great takeaway essentially when you're thinking about startup ideas, make sure there's some connection to something unique to you where you have some unfair advantage. This makes me think about Brian Armstrong. I saw him do a talk once and he gave this really amazing insight about why Coinbase did well and why he started Coinbase. And it's because if you look at his background, he had this really rare Venn diagram of background of computer science and I think it was cryptography and economics, which is the exact set of skills you need to start something like Coinbase. So I think the tip there is just what is that unique Venn diagram of skills in your background and just ideally what you're building connects to that and gives you an unfair advantage.
turns.zh: 好，这是一个很好的收获——基本上当你在想创业点子的时候，要确保它跟你身上某种独特的东西有联系，让你有某种不公平优势。这让我想起 Brian Armstrong。我看过他一次演讲，他讲了一个关于为什么 Coinbase 做得好、他为什么创立 Coinbase 的非常精彩的洞察。是因为如果你看他的背景，他有计算机科学、密码学和经济学这三个领域的一个非常罕见的维恩图交集——而这正是创办 Coinbase 这类公司所需要的技能组合。所以我觉得那个建议就是：你背景里那个独特的技能维恩图是什么？最好你做的东西跟那个有联系，给你一个不公平优势。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Well, yeah. I just met another UVic student at the local university student. She is interested in marketing and so she's gone out and she's found some local clients, so small restaurants and stuff and managed their social media and she said, "Yeah, it's okay. I can make a thousand bucks a month, but it's a lot of work," and the owners really want a lot for their money. And I said, "Well, if you just pivot that idea just ever so slightly, and instead of doing restaurants, you did realtors or wealth managers who have quite a large marketing budget and are used to spending serious money and it only has to work a little bit to make a lot of money for them. Those people, you can charge $5,000 a month." (00:16:44): So I think often it's you find your passion, your skill set, you zero in, and then you just kind of pivot and you find the most profitable way to do it. When I started my web design firm, I started mostly with local and small projects, but very quickly I found a job board in San Francisco where startups would share projects they needed help with. I could charge five times the amount for five times less work.
turns.zh: 对，是的。我最近又遇到一个 UVic 的学生，本地大学的学生。她对营销感兴趣，就出去找了一些本地客户，小餐厅之类的，帮他们管社交媒体。她说：'嗯，还行，我一个月能赚 1000 块，但活很多'，而且老板们花了钱就想要很多东西。我说：'你只要把这个点子稍微转一点点，别做餐厅了，去做房产经纪人或财富经理——他们有相当大的营销预算，习惯花真金白银，而且只要稍微起一点作用就能给他们赚很多钱。这种客户，你可以收 5000 美元一个月。'(00:16:44)：所以我觉得往往是这样的：找到你的热情、你的技能，聚焦进去，然后稍微转一下，找到最赚钱的做法。当我开我的网页设计公司时，我一开始主要做本地小项目，但很快我在旧金山找到一个 job board，创业公司会在上面发布需要帮助的项目。我可以收五倍的价格，做五分之一的工作量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This point about fish where the fish are I think is really important. You can start something that's awesome that you love, that you're so excited about, but nobody needs it. Talk a bit more about just what that looks like. What have you seen when you're thinking about ideas that tell you that there's fish but also not overfished as you pointed out?
turns.zh: 关于'到有鱼的地方钓鱼'这一点我觉得很重要。你可以做一个你觉得很棒、你很喜欢、你超兴奋的东西，但没人需要它。多讲讲这看起来是什么样的。当你在想点子的时候，你怎么判断那里有鱼、但又没被过度捕捞？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: I think it's hard like Warren Buffett has this great quote, "I'm a better businessman because I'm an investor and I'm a better investor because I'm a businessman." And I feel like in order to know what problems are valuable to solve, you kind of need to have valuable problems. So it's a bit of a hard thing because I remember when I was like 20, I would say, I hate how all the cat furniture I can buy for my cats is I bet people would pay a lot of money to solve this, but I didn't understand anything about the realities of that business model. I didn't understand how little people were actually willing to pay. I didn't have a enough life experience to go, "Yes, that's actually a worthwhile opportunity." And I think that being able to know what people would pay to solve the problem realistically is incredibly valuable. (00:18:20): So my example of a realtor selling a house, because I've studied that industry, I know that a realtor can make like 20 to $50,000 selling a single house. So I can intuit that they'd be willing to spend a lot of money if I have a unique way of getting them clients that'll buy houses that'll convert at a high conversion rate that is worth $5,000 a lead maybe, right? So I think you kind of have to understand the problem in depth before you really know. Because when I was starting out, I would go down every rabbit trail, every infomercial idea I had I would think was genius.
turns.zh: 这很难，就像 Warren Buffett 有句名言：'我是更好的商人，因为我是投资人；我是更好的投资人，因为我是商人。'我觉得，要知道哪些问题值得解决，你 kinda 需要自己有有价值的问题。这有点难，因为我记得我 20 岁的时候会说，我讨厌我给猫买的猫家具都那么丑，我打赌人们会花很多钱来解决这个问题，但我根本不理解那个商业模式的现实。我不理解人们实际愿意花多少钱。我没有足够的人生经验去判断'对，那确实是个值得做的机会'。我觉得能够现实地知道人们愿意花多少钱来解决一个问题，是非常有价值的。(00:18:20)：所以我那个房产经纪人卖房的例子——因为我研究过那个行业，我知道一个经纪人卖一套房能赚 2 万到 5 万美元。所以我能直觉地判断，如果我有一种独特的方式能给他带来会买房的客户、转化率很高，那他愿意花很多钱——也许一个线索值 5000 美元，对吧？所以我觉得你必须先深入理解这个问题，才能真正知道。因为当我刚开始的时候，我会顺着每一条兔子洞走下去，每一个电视购物式的点子我都觉得是天才。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Or people, I don't know, that don't have this experience, which is most people. Is there one thing you do, maybe a heuristic that gives you a sense, maybe there's something here, maybe there's a lot of fish, maybe it's a value of prompt or no, the soul tell me it probably isn't.
turns.zh: 或者那些——我不知道——没有这种经验的人，也就是大多数人。有没有一件事是你做的，可能是一个启发式判断，让你感觉'这里可能有东西'或者'鱼很多'或者'这是个有价值的提示'，还是说没有，凭直觉告诉我大概不是？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: No, unfortunately, I think it's mostly gut. I mean Munger and Buffett talk about having a whole bunch of mental models in your brain and they form a latticework, right? And they all kind of piece together. And I feel like for me, there's so much of this that is, it's almost like I'm an AI model and I've trained on all this data of what works and what doesn't and what's a good moat and what's a bad business, et cetera. And when I see it, I just immediately know. I mean, I think all entrepreneurs are so lucky now to be able to go into Claude or ChatGPT and just say, "Hey, I'm thinking about starting a Botox clinic. Can you break down the numbers? Is this a good business? What's hard about it? What is the regulatory moat? What would my payroll look like?" I didn't have any of that and so I started so many incredibly stupid businesses, but I think there's no excuse at this point. You should be able to do it with AI.
turns.zh: 没有，不幸的是，我觉得 mostly 是凭直觉。Munger 和 Buffett 说在脑子里装一大堆心智模型，它们形成一个格栅，对吧？它们都互相拼接在一起。我觉得对我来说，这件事有太多了——几乎就像我是个 AI 模型，我已经在所有这些数据上训练过了——什么有效、什么无效、什么是好的护城河、什么是坏的生意等等。当我看到的时候，我立刻就知道。我的意思是，我觉得所有创业者现在都太幸运了，可以进 Claude 或 ChatGPT 然后说：'嘿，我想开一家肉毒杆菌诊所，你能帮我拆解一下数字吗？这是好生意吗？难在哪里？监管护城河是什么？我的薪酬大概长什么样？'我那时候什么都没有，所以我开了无数个蠢到不行的公司，但我觉得现在已经没有借口了。你应该能用 AI 做到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really good tip actually. Then there's this point you made about boring is good. That's a really good piece of advice. A lot of people are going after flashy stuff, things they condemn on Twitter. Your advice here is boring is actually a really good thing because fewer people are going after it. Is that the general tip?
turns.zh: 这真是个很好的建议。然后你还提到一个点——无聊是好的。这是个很好的建议。很多人都在追那些花哨的东西，那些在 Twitter 上被吹捧的东西。你的建议是无聊其实是个很好的事情，因为追的人少。这是那个大致的建议吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Totally. I mean, so I started this business, one of my first called Flow and Flow was basically Asana before Asana came out. So it was a way to manage your to-do's and projects with your team in a web app and we basically did the thing. We made the mistake that so many entrepreneurs make, which is to go after an industry that everybody goes after just like cafes. Everybody has the idea, man, I wish I could design my own project management system or my own to-do system. And not only that, but everybody loves new things. They love jumping around. I know me personally, in the last three years, I've probably used three different productivity systems and I love jumping around in them and I didn't understand that and I ended up losing $10 million trying to compete with venture-backed businesses and bootstrapping. (00:21:17): It was all my own money, poured $10 million, lit it on fire trying to compete with Asana because I didn't understand how the business world worked really as they had raised hundreds of millions of dollars and they were run by the co-founder of Facebook and it was a little bit like, I'm Fiji and I'm deciding I'm going to invade the United States in retrospect, just completely silly. Now on the flip side, if I'd taken that same amount of energy and I'd instead focused on, let's see, what's a really boring one I've heard about, there was a business I saw recently. (00:21:52): They were making $30 million a year and all they did was help people fill out forms to get government assistance in certain programs. So it'd be like your uncle is disabled and you need to access government funding. The process to do it is incredibly time-consuming and miserable and you have to fill out all these forms. They just have software that fills out the forms for you and it says, look, you're going to get $20,000 as a grant, pay us a thousand bucks, and that is such a boring, nobody wakes up and goes, "I want to make form filling software," but I think they would if they could make 20 million a year
turns.zh: 完全正确。我开了这家公司，我最早的公司之一叫 Flow，Flow 基本上就是 Asana 出来之前的 Asana。它是一个在网页 App 里跟团队一起管理待办和项目的工具，我们基本上做了一件事——犯了很多创业者都会犯的错，就是去追一个所有人都追的行业，就像咖啡馆一样。每个人都有这个想法：'哎，要是我能设计自己的项目管理系统或自己的待办系统多好'。不仅如此，每个人都喜欢新东西，喜欢跳来跳去。我知道我自己——在过去三年里大概换了三种不同的生产力系统，我喜欢换来换去——我不理解这一点，结果我赔了 1000 万美元去跟那些有风投支持的公司竞争，而我是 bootstrap 的。(00:21:17)：全是我的钱，砸了 1000 万，点火烧掉，去跟 Asana 竞争，因为我根本不理解商业世界是怎么运作的——他们融了数亿美元，由 Facebook 的联合创始人运营——这有点像我是斐济，然后我决定要入侵美国，回过头来看简直傻透了。但反过来，如果我把同样的精力放在——让我想想，我最近听说的一个很无聊的——有一家公司我最近看到的。(00:21:52)：他们一年赚 3000 万美元，而他们做的全部事情就是帮人填表格去申请政府援助项目。比如你叔叔残疾了，你需要申请政府资金，流程极其耗时、极其痛苦，要填一堆表格。他们就是有一个帮你填表格的软件，然后说：'看，你能拿到 2 万美元的补助，付我们 1000 块。'这是如此无聊的一门生意，没有人会醒来然后说'我想做填表软件'，但我觉得他们做得很好。所以我觉得'无聊是好的'，少一点花哨，多一点实际。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines of just bad ideas, things people shouldn't start, what are a few ideas that you think everyone thinks is going to be a great idea and then they do it and then they always fail?
turns.zh: 就着这个'坏点子'的思路——哪些事情人们不应该做——有哪几个点子是你觉得所有人都以为会是个好点子，但做了之后总是失败？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Well, I think the biggest mistake, I can speak from my own experience, the biggest mistakes I've made business-wise have been going into business models where other people have repeatedly failed and thinking, I can do this better. So for example, me and one of my best friends about 10 years ago, we really wanted to start a bar. We just thought it'd be so cool to have a bar where us and all of our friends could go, we thought it'd be great for the city. We thought we can run this really high margin because we're tech guys, we know how to build systems, we're good at business, and we were utterly humbled. We realized that we didn't know anything about business compared to someone who runs a pizzeria. If you think about it, like my example earlier of if you run a software company, what has to happen? (00:23:24): You have to hire a bunch of nerds, they need internet connections and computers and you need to pay them and you need to coordinate online and everyone can work asynchronously. Nothing has to go right. It's not that complicated, at least at small-scale. A pizzeria, it's like if the baker doesn't wake up at three in the morning and start prepping dough, the entire thing is effed and all along the way there's a hundred different failure points from front of house, back of house, the deliveries, arriving on time, all this logistics. And so I think it's been stuff like that. I mean also I got into the news business, the local news business. I ended up buying an old paper in Vancouver and it's the exact same thing. It's like you can't take a brilliant management team and change a bad business model. Ultimately the business model wins.
turns.zh: 我觉得最大的错误——我可以从自己的经验来说——我在商业上犯过的最大错误，就是进入那些别人已经反复失败过的商业模式，然后心里想着'我能做得更好'。比如，大概 10 年前，我和我最好的朋友之一真的很想开一家酒吧。我们就觉得有一家我们自己和朋友都能去的酒吧太酷了，对城市也好。我们觉得能运营得很高毛利，因为我们是搞科技的，知道怎么建系统，擅长做生意——结果我们被彻底打脸了。我们意识到，跟一个开披萨店的人比起来，我们对做生意一无所知。你想想，我之前那个例子——如果你开一家软件公司，需要什么？(00:23:24)：你得雇一堆 nerd，他们需要网络和电脑，你得付他们工资，你得在线协调，大家都可以异步工作。没什么必须特别顺利的，至少小规模上没那么复杂。但披萨店呢，如果面包师凌晨三点不起来和面，整个事情就完蛋了，而且一路上有一百个不同的失败点——前厅、后厨、送货准时到达、所有这些物流。所以我觉得就是这类东西。我还做过新闻生意，本地新闻。我最后买了温哥华的一家老报纸，完全一样的道理——你没法拿一个出色的管理团队去改变一个糟糕的商业模式。最终赢的是商业模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is really good advice. Basically if there's a bunch of dead bodies in that space, there's probably something there that keeps killing them that you're probably not aware of until maybe somebody figures something out, right? Once in a while, once in a blue moon, someone's like, "Okay, here's how we do this and then it works."
turns.zh: 这真是很好的建议。基本上如果一个赛道里有一堆尸体，那大概有某种东西在不断地杀死他们，你大概没意识到——直到有人搞清楚怎么做，对吧？偶尔一次，千载难逢，有人说'好，我们这样做，然后就成了'。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Well, look at Instacart. When Instacart came out, everyone said, "Well, Webvan failed. This is never going to work." And we still don't necessarily know if Instacart is a great business. I don't know, I haven't studied it, but I think it was like, okay, enough technology has changed that it can happen, but would it be easier to start Instacart, Amazon or Coupang or would it be easier to start an enterprise SaaS software company? Definitely the enterprise SaaS software company.
turns.zh: 你看 Instacart。Instacart 出来的时候，所有人都说：'Webvan 失败了，这永远行不通。'我们现在也还不一定知道 Instacart 是不是个好生意。我不知道，我没研究过，但我觉得大概是——好吧，技术变化够了，所以它可以发生了。但是，做 Instacart、Amazon 或 Coupang 更容易，还是做一家企业级 SaaS 软件公司更容易？肯定是企业级 SaaS 软件公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see. So this is I guess is the advice there. The thing that is easy to start is the thing you should not do because everyone's going after that.
turns.zh: 我明白了。所以这就是那个建议：容易开始的事情是你不应该做的，因为所有人都在追那个。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Well, it goes back to my gym analogy of if you're going to deadlift 300 pounds, trained for 15 years, you should have already had three startups and they should have worked and you've really built up the reps. And I think that if I was going to start Instacart, that's different than someone who's 20 starting it. Not that I would be good at it, but at least I would know what I'm getting into.
turns.zh: 嗯，这又回到我那个健身房的比喻——如果你要硬拉 300 磅，你已经训练了 15 年，你应该已经有过三个创业公司都成功了，你已经真正积累了足够的 reps。我觉得如果我要做 Instacart，那跟一个 20 岁的人去做是不一样的。不是说我会做得好，但至少我知道我在进入什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about something that is this endless debate on Twitter. Maybe it's a false dichotomy between lifestyle businesses, bootstrap businesses, this idea of not raising money, just making revenue, living off the revenue versus venture-backed venture scale companies feels like you're very good at the first bucket and a lot of people, this is their dream, "I'm just going to start something. I'll start a lifestyle business, make a few million a year, never raise money. Who needs VCs? VCs suck." Advice for deciding which route to go with an idea you have.
turns.zh: 我们来聊一个在 Twitter 上永远在辩论的话题。也许这是个伪二元对立——生活方式生意、bootstrap 生意，就是不融资、靠收入活着、靠收入过日子，对立于有风投支持的、风险规模的公司。感觉你非常擅长第一类，很多人这是他们的梦想：'我就做点什么，开个生活方式公司，一年赚几百万，永远不融资。谁需要 VC？VC 烂透了。'关于如何决定走哪条路，你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Well, I think it's just not true that a "lifestyle" or bootstrap business can't get huge. I mean, we bootstrapped the entire business and now across all of our companies we do almost $300 million in revenue. And the whole time I had been focusing on taking, starting small businesses, small ideas, simple ideas, often buying small companies and watching them grow really big. And I think that the only difference between what we do and what a venture capitalist does is the level of tolerance of burning money on fire. And I just haven't seen that If we choose the right businesses that aren't in incredibly competitive markets or where they have some sort of moat. So what I mean by that is a great brand or a network effect like a social network or something like that, I don't feel we're holding them back by not letting them light up a bunch of money on fire because these things naturally grow. (00:27:12): The numbers, I mean they're like balloons, they just go as long as we don't mess them up too much. So I think the decision ultimately comes down to how hairy do you want your big, hairy, audacious goal to be? And if your big, hairy, audacious goal is I'm going to start the next satellite business that creates some sort of crazy technological revolution. Yes, you're going to have to raise a venture capital unless you're already a billionaire or something like that. But if you're wanting to just tinker and solve a problem that you think is not going to be hyper-competitive, so for example, that form-filling thing or software that just does a narrow thing that doesn't require 20, 30, 40 million to be lit on fire before it can make money, then you can have a wonderful life and build a wonderful company that can scale into the hundreds of millions of dollars if you play your cards right without ever raising money.
turns.zh: 我觉得'生活方式'或 bootstrap 的生意做不到很大这个说法就是不成立的。我是说，我们整个生意都是 bootstrap 的，现在我们所有公司加起来收入接近 3 亿美元。整个过程我都在专注于做小生意、小点子、简单的点子，经常是收购小公司然后看着它们变大。我觉得我们做的和风投做的唯一区别，就是烧钱的容忍度。我没看到——如果我们选对了生意，不在那些竞争极其激烈的市场，或者它们有某种护城河。我的意思是，比如一个伟大的品牌，或者像社交网络那样的网络效应——我不觉得我们不让他们烧钱是在拖后腿，因为这些东西会自然增长。(00:27:12)：数字嘛，它们就像气球，只要我们不太搞砸，它们就会一直涨。所以我觉得这个决定最终归结于：你想要你的'宏大、毛茸茸、大胆的目标'有多毛茸茸？如果你的宏大目标是我要做下一个卫星生意，创造某种疯狂的技术革命——是的，你将不得不融风投，除非你已经是亿万富翁之类的。但如果你只是想鼓捣一下、解决一个你觉得不会过度竞争的问题——比如那个填表的事，或者一个只做很窄的事情、不需要烧掉两三千万才能赚钱的软件——那你完全可以有一个美好的人生，建一家美好的公司，如果打牌打得好，可以做到数亿美元规模，而永远不需要融资。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Per the story you shared with Flow where you're competing against a venture-funded company, if there is a venture-backed company in this space, is the advice you're not going to win competing with them most likely and try to do something else.
turns.zh: 根据你分享的 Flow 那个故事——你跟一家有风投支持的公司竞争——如果一个赛道里已经有一家风投支持的公司，你的建议是：你大概率赢不了跟他们的竞争，所以去做别的？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Well, look at Things. Do you know Things?
turns.zh: 你看 Things。你知道 Things 吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have used Things
turns.zh: 我用过 Things。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: I do too. It's awesome. Things still exist and Things has existed for 20 years. It's run by I believe one or two or three people. It's not a big team, certainly under 10 people, it was, I believe, bootstrapped and it's just consistently delivered an exceptional product and built up a loyal following. They have their 10,000 true fans who use it, and that's enough for them, but they don't do a lot. They've been very intentional. They don't do any AI stuff, they don't have an API. They're not on Android. They're very focused and I think they have succeeded. But the question is, what would an MBA or a business professor say about their success? If the measure of success is did they maximize taking as much market share as possible and grow to be as big as possible, then the answer is no because Asana and other people have built multi-billion dollar companies. (00:29:28): If the goal is the founder has an incredible life, probably has three houses, flies all over the place, does whatever he wants, has recurring revenue and he gets to work with headphones on building beautiful piece of software that people love, then I think he's won. I am generally much more in the camp of the Things guy has won, not Dustin Moskovitz. Dustin Moskovitz is just playing a different game than the Things guy. And if Dustin Moskovitz was running Things, he'd be miserable and if the Things guy was running Asana, he would probably kill himself because he wants to put his headphones on and build.
turns.zh: 我也用。它超棒。Things 还活着，而且已经存在 20 年了。我记得是由一两个人或者三个人运营的。团队不大，肯定不到 10 个人，我记得是 bootstrap 的，一直持续地产出卓越的产品，建立了一批忠实的用户。他们有他们的 1 万个铁粉，这对他们来说就够了。但他们做得不多，他们非常有意识——不做 AI，没有 API，不在 Android 上。他们非常专注，我觉得他们成功了。但问题是：一个 MBA 或商学院教授会怎么说他们的成功？如果成功的衡量标准是'是否最大化地夺取市场份额并尽可能地做大'，那答案是否定的，因为 Asana 和其他人已经建了数十亿美元的公司。(00:29:28)：如果目标是创始人有一个美好的人生——大概有三套房子，满世界飞，想做什么做什么，有经常性收入，可以戴着耳机构建人们喜爱的美丽软件——那我觉得他赢了。我通常更倾向于 Things 那个家伙赢了，而不是 Dustin Moskovitz。Dustin Moskovitz 跟 Things 那个家伙玩的是不同的游戏。如果 Dustin Moskovitz 来管 Things，他会很痛苦；如果 Things 那个家伙来管 Asana，他大概会想自杀，因为他想戴着耳机做产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wonder why nobody has come. It feels like just with lifestyle businesses, if it's working and you would think somebody would come in with more money and more funding and just eat their lunch, is the key that the market is too small for a VC to ever be excited and so that's why no one's coming for them?
turns.zh: 我很好奇为什么没人来。感觉就是生活方式生意如果做得好，你会觉得有人会带着更多的钱和更多的融资进来抢他们的饭碗——关键是市场太小，VC 永远不会兴奋，所以没人来抢？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: I think so. I mean, I think Things probably, I'm just guessing, I don't know any of the numbers or whatever, but I would assume it makes between five and $25 million of revenue, which to a VC is not even worth considering a VC. For a VC to invest in your business, you need to have a story where it's worth 300 million to a billion dollars or more. So it's just not that exciting to them, which again, going back to fish where the fish are, you don't want to be fighting against the commercial fishermen. If you just want to have a little business where you get enough fish to feed your family and your village or whatever, find the other fishing hole. Don't go where the trawlers are.
turns.zh: 我觉得是。我是说 Things 大概——我只是在猜，我不知道任何数字——但我估计它的收入在 500 万到 2500 万美元之间，这对 VC 来说甚至不值得考虑。VC 要投你的生意，你需要有一个值 3 亿到 10 亿美元以上的故事。所以这对他们来说就是不够兴奋。这又回到'到有鱼的地方钓鱼'——你不想跟商业渔夫去抢。如果你只是想有个小生意，钓足够的鱼养活你的家人和你的村子之类的，那就去找另一个钓鱼洞。别去拖网渔船去的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is great advice if you're trying to start a non venture backed company is find. This metaphor just keeps working for us, which is fish where the fish are, but not where the professional fishermen are. Also, ideally not where there's just a ton of, I don't know, fishermen from all over the place. I don't know, solopreneur fishermen. Okay. Coming back to just starting a successful company, what would you say are the keys to an amazing business model, an amazing business broadly, what should you be thinking about and looking into? I know you spent a lot of time thinking about this. When you're buying companies, what are a few bullet points that you want to focus on?
turns.zh: 这是很好的建议——如果你要开一家非风投支持的公司，就找……这个比喻一直对我们有用——到有鱼的地方钓鱼，但别去专业渔夫去的地方。理想情况下也别去一堆——我不知道——到处都是的渔夫去的地方，那种个体户渔夫。好的，回到开一家成功的公司这个话题——你认为一个出色的商业模式、一个出色的生意的关键是什么？你应该思考什么、关注什么？我知道你花了很多时间思考这个。你买公司的时候，有哪几个要点是你会关注的？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: What I do for a living is basically buy businesses. So in my early career I started one business, then I started about 10 more, and then I realized starting businesses was extremely hard and I was doing pretty well. I was making quite a bit of money and I'd sold one of my businesses and I was looking out at the next 10 years and really asking myself what do I want my career to be and am I happy doing what I'm doing? And the answer was no. I did not starting businesses and experiencing that failure rate, it was incredibly stressful. And so I picked up a book about investing and I got lucky. The first one I bought was about Warren Buffett, and for those that don't know, Warren Buffett is he's counter to every VC kind of hustle culture thing you might hear because he basically just sits quietly in a room and reads all day, despite owning 260 different businesses and being one of the 10 wealthiest people in the world, his life is incredibly calm. (00:32:44): He only does what he wants and he spends most of his time quietly reading and once or twice a year, he makes a big decision to buy a business. And so when I read about Warren Buffett, I just thought, wow, I'm a sucker. I'm running around like a crazy person trying to run all these businesses. Why am I not just buying businesses and letting them run? And so when I'm buying a business, what I'm really looking for is something that I can't mess up. Right now, obviously we buy a business, we try not to mess it up, and we're very intentional, actually very odd in that when Tiny buys a company, we generally just leave them alone. If they already have management in place, we say nothing changes, no one should know that we've even bought them. Obviously people know that, but really there should be no change whatsoever. (00:33:31): The only change that we generally make is if the founder wants to leave the business, then we'll bring in a CEO to run the company, and that's probably the most important decision that we make. So I'm looking for a business though where it is so good that it's hard to mess up, and most businesses are very easy to mess up. One person leaves and the whole business falls apart because it's held together with dental floss and duct tape. And so I'm really looking for what Warren Buffett would call a moat. So a moat is basically a brand, so that could be a brand like Coca-Cola, Tylenol, Advil, something like that. So something that gives you pricing power where you can consistently charge and you have loyal customers or where we usually find a lot of opportunity is in network effects. (00:34:23): So typically we're looking for a community that's gotten so big where people don't want to go elsewhere. So for example, we own Letterboxd, which is the largest social network for film lovers. And the question is, if someone else wants to compete with us, why would someone go to their social network that has a small number of users when all their friends are already on Letterboxd? And so you see that same kind of thing with Instagram or Facebook or similar. And so we're looking for businesses like that, something that has staying power that is hard to compete with and that we can hold over the very long term.
turns.zh: 我做的就是买公司。在我早期职业生涯中我开了一家公司，然后又开了大概 10 家，然后我意识到开公司极其困难，而我做得还不错。我赚了相当多的钱，卖掉了一家公司，然后我展望未来 10 年，真的在问自己：我想让我的职业生涯是什么样的？我做现在的事开心吗？答案是不。我不再享受开公司了，经历那种失败率太有压力了。于是我拿起一本关于投资的书，运气不错，第一本就是关于 Warren Buffett 的。对于那些不知道的人，Warren Buffett 跟你听到的所有 VC 那种奋斗文化正好相反——他基本上就是安静地坐在一个房间里读一整天的书，尽管他拥有 260 家不同的公司，是世界上最富有的 10 个人之一。他的生活难以置信地平静。(00:32:44)：他只做他想做的事，大部分时间安静地读书，一年做一两次大决定去收购一家公司。当我读到 Warren Buffett 的时候，我就想：哇，我是个冤大头。我像个疯子一样跑来跑去管这堆公司，为什么我不直接买公司然后让它们自己运行？所以我买公司的时候，我真正在找的是某种我搞不砸的东西。显然我们买了一家公司的时会尽量不搞砸，我们非常有意——其实在 Tiny 买公司时我们通常就是放任不管，这一点很奇怪。如果他们已经有管理团队在位，我们就说什么都不变，没人应该知道我们收购了他们。显然人们会知道，但真的不应该有任何变化。(00:33:31)：我们通常做的唯一改变是，如果创始人想离开公司，那我们就引入一位 CEO 来运营，这可能是我做的最重要的决定。但除此之外，我们就是放手。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It was interesting when Elon bought X, how that was such a test of the power of network effects. If you think about it, back then he changed the name. So the brand completely changed the team. 80% of the people left. What was left, it was the network and the network effect and the simplest way. Just for folks that aren't super familiar with network effects, the way I think about it is just network effect is where every additional user that joins the network becomes more useful for everybody.
turns.zh: Elon 收购 X 的时候很有意思，那真是对网络效应力量的一次测试。你想想，他改了名字，品牌完全变了，团队 80% 的人走了。剩下的是什么？就是网络和网络效应，最简单的方式。对于那些不太熟悉网络效应的人，我理解的方式是：网络效应就是每多一个用户加入网络，对所有人来说都变得更有用。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: There's another moat, which is high switching costs, which I don't really like because it's not really very consumer friendly, but an example might be Salesforce where no one wants to, they've spent years and they've done all the implementation and trained everyone on it, and it's kind of the standard, everybody hates it, but ripping it out and switching is such a pain in the that they just won't bother. That's another form of sometimes a great business, but again, that's more depressing. I don't love that one.
turns.zh: 还有另一种护城河是高切换成本，我不太喜欢这种，因为它对消费者不太友好。但例子可能是 Salesforce——没人愿意，他们已经花了几年做实施、培训了所有人，它 kinda 是标准了，每个人都讨厌它，但拆掉换掉它太麻烦了，所以他们就不折腾了。那是另一种有时候是伟大生意的形式，但同样，这更令人沮丧。我不喜欢这种。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the last company you guys bought?
turns.zh: 你们买的最新的公司是哪家？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: We bought Serato. Serato is the largest DJ software company in the world. So if you ever see a DJ playing and they've got a laptop in front of them, probably using Serato to DJ.
turns.zh: 我们买了 Serato。Serato 是世界上最大的 DJ 软件公司。所以如果你看到一个 DJ 在表演，前面有台笔记本，那大概用的就是 Serato。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that is super cool. What I'd like a funding to be walking into.
turns.zh: 哇，这超酷。这听起来是我很想投的那种。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: I used to DJ so I was aware of them and it was one of those moments we talked about earlier where I understood the business. They had a really interesting mode of this huge passionate user base and deep hardware integration. And I also love DJing and I was able to analyze the business and luck comes to the prepared mind and it worked out.
turns.zh: 我以前做 DJ，所以我认识他们，这是我们之前聊过的那种时刻——我理解这门生意。他们有一个非常有趣的模式：一群庞大而热情的用户群，还有深度的硬件整合。我也爱 DJ，我能分析这门生意，机会青睐有准备的头脑，就成了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is another great callback to your excellent piece of advice of just ideally what you're working on, whether you're starting the company or buying the company, is you have a unique unfair advantage or some kind of unique background that connects to that idea. Let me ask you one more question before we shift a whole different topic, hint, hint, AI. Something that I know you talk a lot about, something you believe strongly and something you deal with a lot is when you buy companies is just as people and the challenges of management and hiring and people. So what have you learned about just how to successfully, I don't know, find amazing people, keep amazing people, help people be more successful within the companies that you operate?
turns.zh: 这又是呼应你那个很好的建议——理想情况下，无论你是开公司还是买公司，你都要有一个独特的不公平优势，或者某种跟那个点子相连的独特背景。让我在换一个完全不同的话题之前——提示一下，AI——再问你一个问题。我知道你经常谈论、深信不疑、也经常处理的一件事，就是你买公司时关于人和管理的挑战。关于怎么成功地找到优秀的人、留住优秀的人、帮助人在你运营的公司里更成功，你学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: My business partner, Chris, has a really great quote. He says, "There are no problems. There is only people problems." And so we've found that you could tell us that there's a disaster that one of our business units is about to fail or something like that. As long as I'm surrounded by really great smart people, I feel fine. But when we have a bad actor, we have a psycho or a narcissist or a really horrible, difficult person we're dealing with, all bets are off and life becomes incredibly stressful. So I'd say I spend probably 20% of my time just trying to make sure we're filtering people very carefully and ensuring we're working with people that we enjoy. And I could talk about it in the AI, I've done some really interesting stuff to help me screen and identify difficult people, but I've just found that the biggest mistake I made in my early career was I would hire people because I liked them on gut and I would think that I could change them. (00:38:12): So it's kind of like in romantic relationships, it never works out well. If you get married to someone and you go, "Okay, well this is going to be a great relationship as long as I can convert them to Christianity or I can change their parents or their personality," or whatever it is. And so I've just found that I've never been able to change someone. You can never mentor someone out into being a good employee. And the kind of heuristic I have is if I ever think, should I fire this person even once, I should fire them immediately. It has always been a signal, at least for me, that when someone's a superstar, I can't imagine firing them. I think it's impossible, I'd be lost without them. (00:38:56): But when I repeatedly start going, "Man, is this person going to work out?" Almost always within six to 12 months, it doesn't work out. And so I really try and be really direct about stuff like that and just cut when it's not working. So I'd say the lesson really is hire for what you need. Don't hire just for potential, which is counter to what a lot of people say. A lot of people say hire for potential and coach them into being whatever you need. I just haven't found that. I think you need to hire someone who already is fully formed and can do what you need. But again, everyone does it differently.
turns.zh: 我的合伙人 Chris 有句很棒的话。他说：'没有问题，只有人的问题。'我们发现，你可以告诉我们某个业务单元要失败了之类的灾难——只要我身边都是很棒、聪明的人，我就没事。但当我们有一个坏分子——一个 psychopath 或 narcissist 或一个非常糟糕、难搞的人——那就什么都没准了，生活变得难以置信地有压力。所以我大概花 20% 的时间就是确保我们非常仔细地过滤人，确保跟我们共事的人是我们喜欢的。我可以在 AI 那块聊聊——我做过一些很有意思的事来帮我筛选和识别难搞的人——但我发现我早期职业生涯最大的错误就是凭直觉喜欢一个人就雇他，然后觉得我能改变他。(00:38:12)：这有点像恋爱关系，如果你跟一个人结婚然后说：'好的，只要我能让他信基督教，或者改变他的父母或他的性格'之类的，这永远不会有好结果。我发现我从来没能改变一个人，你永远没法把一个人指导成一个好员工。我的一个启发式法则是：如果我哪怕想过一次'我是不是该炒掉这个人'，我就应该立刻炒掉他。这对我来说一直是一个信号——当一个人是超级明星的时候，我无法想象炒掉他，我觉得不可能，没他我会迷失。(00:38:56)：但当 我反复开始想'哎，这个人能不能行'的时候，几乎总是 6 到 12 个月内就不行了。所以我真的尽量在这种事上非常直接，不行就砍。所以我觉得教训就是——为你的需要而雇人。不要为潜力而雇人，这跟很多人说的相反。很多人说为潜力雇人然后把他指导成你需要的样子。我就是没看到这个。我觉得你需要雇一个已经成型、能做你需要的事的人。但同样，每个人做法不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is big advice. Powerful advice. Is this true not just for the CEOs of the companies you run? As for folks under lower down the ladder too?
turns.zh: 这是很大的建议，很有力量的建议。这不仅仅适用于你管的那些公司的 CEO 吗？也适用于更下层的人吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Well, for CEOs, one of the most interesting things we've observed is, so I'll give you an example. We had a CEO come in and we were interviewing them and in my opinion, the business needed to grow via organic marketing. In his opinion, it was enterprise sales. And so when we're interviewing him, he keeps going back to his experience building with enterprise sales. And there's this great saying, "To a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail." And so for him, he's looking at this business and going enterprise sales, that's the way to grow. I hire him, but I say, "Look, if we're going to hire you, we need you to do the organic marketing." Lo and behold, of course, he goes off and he does the enterprise sales thing. And I've just found that hiring CEOs is like they're an elephant and you're the rider. (00:40:31): They're going to go wherever it is that they want to go. And so listening incredibly carefully to people's words and their experiences, because generally people will do the thing they tell you. So what I look for when I interview a CEO now, I want to be nodding along. I want to go, that's exactly what I would do or that's way smarter than my idea. And then I just leave them alone because I've found that anytime I try and pull them in a certain direction or coach them or whatever, it just doesn't work. And again, this could be my problem. I might be the world's worst coach and mentor, but for me, that's been what's true.
turns.zh: 嗯，对于 CEO，我们观察到的最有意思的事情之一是——我给你举个例子。我们面试过一个 CEO，在我看来，那个业务需要通过自然增长营销来成长。在他的观念里，是企业销售。我们面试他的时候，他一直回到他做企业销售的经验上。有一句很好的话：'对手拿锤子的人来说，一切都像钉子。'所以他看这个业务，就 goes 企业销售才是增长的方式。我雇了他，但我说：'看，我们要雇你的话，我们需要你做自然增长营销。'果不其然，他出去就做了企业销售那套。我发现雇 CEO 就像——他们是大象，你是骑手。(00:40:31)：他们要去哪就去哪。所以非常仔细地听人们说的话和他们的经验，因为人们通常会做他们告诉你他们会做的事。所以我现在面试 CEO 时寻找的是，我想一路点头，我想说'那正是我会做的'或者'那比我的主意聪明多了'。然后我就放他不管。因为我发现每次我试图把他们拉向某个方向或指导他们之类的，就是没用。再说，这可能是我自己的问题。我可能是世界上最差的教练和导师，但对我来说，这是真的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine there's also an element of they won't love the job if they want to be doing say enterprise sales, and then they're creating viral TikTok videos all day and tweeting. They're like, "What the hell?"
turns.zh: 我猜还有一个元素是，他们也不会喜欢这份工作——如果他们想做企业销售，然后整天在那里做病毒式 TikTok 视频和发推，他们会觉得'这搞什么？'

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Well, I've also found people will shoot themselves in the foot. If I tell them an idea in a board meeting and I say, "I really need you to try this," it never works because usually they sandbag it, right? They don't really put their heart into it or they're just placating me and they don't want it to work. They want their idea to work. And so I've learned not to do that.
turns.zh: 嗯，我也发现人们会搬起石头砸自己的脚。如果我在董事会上给他们一个主意，我说'我真的需要你试试这个'，这永远没用，因为他们通常会 sandbag，对吧？他们不是真心投入，或者只是敷衍我，他们不希望它成功。他们希望他们自己的主意成功。所以我学会了不那样做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Miro. Every day new headlines are scaring us about all the ways that AI is coming for our jobs, creating a lot of anxiety and fear. But a recent survey for Miro tells a different story. 76% of people believe that AI can benefit their role, but over 50% of people struggle to know when to use it. Enter Miro's innovation Workspace, an intelligent platform that brings people and AI together in a shared space to get great work done. Miro has been empowering teams to transform bold ideas into the next big thing for over a decade. Today, they're at the forefront of bringing products to market even faster by unleashing the combined power of AI and human potential. Teams can work with Miro AI to turn unstructured data like sticky notes or screenshots into usable diagrams, product briefs, data tables, and prototypes in minutes. (00:42:26): You don't have to be an AI master or to toggle yet another tool. The work you're already doing in Miro's canvas is the prompt. Help your teams get great work done with Miro. Check it out at Miro.com to find out how. That's M-I-R-O.com. (00:42:41): Let's talk about AI. It's so funny to watch you on Twitter. Clearly you've become AI obsessed, AIphile. I don't know what the term is, and I love that you're not just the kind of person that just talks about it and tweets pontifications, you're clearly using it in every facet of your job and looking for more ways to use AI. So I have a lot of questions here because I think this is where more and more founders are going to be where you are today. First of all, just what's in your AI stack these days? What are the tools you find yourself coming back to most or finding most useful?
turns.zh: 本期节目由 Miro 赞助。每天都有新的头条新闻吓唬我们，说 AI 要来抢我们的工作了，制造了很多焦虑和恐惧。但 Miro 最近的一项调查讲了不同的故事。76% 的人相信 AI 能让他们的工作受益，但超过 50% 的人不知道什么时候该用它。这就是 Miro 的创新工作空间登场的地方——一个把人和 AI 聚集在共享空间里完成出色工作的智能平台。Miro 十多年来一直在赋能团队把大胆的想法变成下一个大事件。今天，他们走在通过释放 AI 和人类潜力的合力来更快把产品推向市场的最前沿。团队可以与 Miro AI 一起工作，把便利贴或截图这样的非结构化数据在几分钟内变成可用的图表、产品简报、数据表和原型。(00:42:26)：你不需要是 AI 大师，也不需要再切换一个工具。你在 Miro 画布上已经在做的工作就是 prompt。帮助你的团队用 Miro 完成出色的工作。去 Miro.com 了解详情。那就是 M-I-R-O.com。(00:42:41)：我们来聊 AI。看你在 Twitter 上的样子真好笑。显然你已经变成了 AI 痴迷者、AI 爱好者——我不知道该用什么词。我喜欢的是你不只是那种只会谈论和发推做空头大论的人，你显然在工作的方方面面都在用 AI，还在找更多使用 AI 的方式。所以我有很多问题，因为我觉得越来越多的创始人会到你现在的位置。首先，你现在的 AI 技术栈里都有什么？你发现自己最常回来用、最有用的工具是什么？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: So the primary tool I use is a tool called Lindy, Lindy.ai. And what it basically lets you do is build workflows and agents. So it's very simple. You might say, "When I get an email in the Gmail API, I want to add an AI agent that reads the email and labels it based on that." Or you can build a crazy Rube Goldberg machine that sends different emails all sorts of different places. So for example, when I get an email and it's related to my kid's school, one of the big problems I have is that my kid's school sends so many emails, the field trip is on Thursday and you need to bring the following things. And meanwhile, there's parent teacher interviews and all these things get added to my calendar. The AI agent automatically takes that, puts it onto my calendar, makes sure there's notes for all the things I need to prepare and stuff. So I have just basically tried to take every single thing a human could do in my inbox and automate it with Lindy.
turns.zh: 我主要用的工具叫 Lindy，Lindy.ai。它基本上让你构建工作流和 agent。很简单，你可以说：'当我在 Gmail API 收到邮件时，我想加一个 AI agent 来读这封邮件并据此给它打标签。'或者你可以建一个疯狂的 Rube Goldberg 机器，把不同的邮件发到各种不同的地方。比如，当我收到一封跟孩子学校相关的邮件——我的一个大问题是孩子的学校发了太多邮件，春游在周四，你需要带以下东西；同时还有家长会等等——所有这些都要加到我的日历里。AI agent 会自动把这些放到我的日历上，确保我需要准备的所有事情都有笔记。所以我基本上就是尝试把一个人能在我收件箱里做的每一件事都用 Lindy 自动化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you're sitting there in Lindy doing this yourself or do you have people that you've trained to help build these sorts of things for you?
turns.zh: 你是自己坐在 Lindy 里做这些，还是你训练了人来帮你构建这些东西？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: No, I do it myself.
turns.zh: 不，我自己做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. How many agents, if that's the term you want to use, do you have running for you roughly?
turns.zh: 好。你大概有多少个 agent——如果想用这个词的话——在为你运行？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Oh man, I think I probably have not a crazy amount within... Let's see. Well, each workflow probably has four or five agents. So for example, my inbox has four or five agents, and then I have a whole bunch of other, I've got a calendar agent, I've got a meeting agent, I've got an email agent, I've got a scheduler, I've got a CRM, and basically they're all different workflows. So the whole bunch of agents within.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪，我想我大概有……不算特别疯狂的数量……让我想想。每个工作流大概有四五个 agent。比如我的收件箱有四五个 agent，然后我还有一大堆其他的——我有日历 agent、会议 agent、邮件 agent、调度器、CRM——基本上它们都是不同的工作流。所以里面有 whole bunch 的 agent。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, and you're not an investor in Lindy, right? You're just a fan, super user.
turns.zh: 好，你不是 Lindy 的投资人吧？你只是个粉丝、超级用户。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: No, no.
turns.zh: 不是，不是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fun fact. I actually am. So this is great.
turns.zh: 有趣的事：我其实是。所以这很棒。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Oh, no way. That's awesome.
turns.zh: 哦，真巧。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Tiny angel investor. So just want to put that out there, which I love that this came up organically. What are a couple other really interesting use cases, workflows you've built that people might be inspired by it?
turns.zh: 小小天使投资人。所以我想把这个说出来，我很喜欢这个是自然冒出来的。还有哪几个非常有趣的使用场景、你构建的工作流，可能会让别人受到启发？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Let me go through the email one a little more. So basically emails come in and the first agent says, does Andrew even need to see this? Let's say you're in a thread and you've already chimed in and everyone's just saying, cool, that works. I don't need to see that. So just archives that never. So that immediately reduces my email by about 20%. Then it decides is this something that is time sensitive? Is this something that needs to be dealt with in the next 24 hours? And if so, it labels it in a special 24-hour label. So when I go in my email, one of the biggest stresses I find is I go, "Shit, there's 200 emails in here, and if I don't go through all of them, I don't know if there's an emergency burning somewhere." So now I do. Then it takes any email or every single email and it decides, is this a simple decision? (00:46:00): So for example, let's say you email me and you say, "Hey, do you want to get lunch?" So it emails me privately and it says, "Hey, Lenny wants to get lunch. Do you want to say yes? Do you want to say yes, but in a few months? Do you want to say no? How do you want to say no?" And it gives me multiple choice. I just can say four, number four, and then it'll email you as me and it'll write out a nice thoughtful email or whatever. So stuff like that is so freaking cool and helpful. And I'd say that it's replaced stuff that my full-time, I used to have a full-time assistant just working on email that's all completely automated and there's all sorts of other cool stuff I'm doing there. Other agents, I'm working on one right now to manage my calendar, which is really complex. I do a lot of scheduling and a lot of rules. I have another really simple one. It adds emojis to every single calendar event. So when I look at my calendar, I've got beautiful little emojis for every single calendar event. Very silly.
turns.zh: 让我把邮件那个再讲多一点。基本上邮件进来，第一个 agent 说：Andrew 需要看这个吗？假设你在一个邮件线程里，你已经发过言了，大家只是在说'好的，行'——我不需要看那个。所以直接归档。这立刻减少了我大概 20% 的邮件。然后它判断这是不是时间敏感的？是不是需要在 24 小时内处理的？如果是，它就打上一个特殊的 24 小时标签。所以我进邮件的时候——我觉得最大的压力之一就是我进去一看：'糟了，这里有 200 封邮件，如果我不全部过一遍，我不知道哪里是不是有紧急的事在烧。'现在我知道了。然后它对每一封邮件判断，这是个简单的决策吗？(00:46:00)：比如，假设你给我发邮件说：'嘿，你想一起吃个午饭吗？'它就私下给我发邮件说：'嘿，Lenny 想吃午饭。你想答应吗？你想答应但推迟几个月吗？你想拒绝吗？你想怎么拒绝？'它给我多选题。我只要说四，数字四，然后它就替我以我的名义给你发邮件，写一封很周到体贴的邮件之类的。这种东西太他妈酷、太有用了。我以前有一个全职助理专门处理邮件——现在全自动化了，我还在那里做各种其他很酷的事。其他 agent，我现在正在做一个管我日历的，我的日历非常复杂，我有很多日程和规则。我还有一个非常简单的，给每一个日历事件加 emoji。这样我看日历的时候，每个事件上都有漂亮的小 emoji。很傻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are the emojis? Do they represent something?
turns.zh: 那些 emoji 代表什么意思吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Yeah, so if I write weightlifting, it'll just do a guy weightlifting or whatever. I've got one that, this one's cool. Basically what it does, every time I email someone, it looks them up online, it figures out what city they live in. It checks my CRM and air table. It says, "Okay, I don't know where do you live."
turns.zh: 是的，比如我写举重，它就放一个举重的小人。我还有一个很酷的，基本上它做的就是，每次我给某人发邮件，它就在网上查这个人，搞清楚他住哪个城市。它检查我的 CRM 和 airtable，然后说：'好吧，你住哪里？'

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In Marin, in the Bay Area.
turns.zh: 在 Marin，湾区。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Okay. So it'd say, "Okay, you email Lenny, he lives in Marin." It puts in the database you live in Marin. And then next time I travel to the Bay Area, the agent will see two weeks before and it'll say, "I saw you're going to San Francisco. Here's all the people in San Francisco you should try and have coffee with." Right? So just all these things that-
turns.zh: 好。它就会说：'好，你给 Lenny 发邮件了，他住在 Marin。'它把'你住在 Marin'放进数据库。然后下次我去湾区，agent 会在两周前看到，然后说：'我看到你要去旧金山。这是旧金山所有你应该试着一起喝杯咖啡的人。'对吧？就是所有这些——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I would pay for that.
turns.zh: 我愿意为这个付费。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, exactly. All these things that I've dreamed of having my assistant do that my assistant could just never consistently do because she gets distracted, we're doing an event, there's something going on. It's like having the world's most reliable employee who costs $200 a month and works 24/7.
turns.zh: 对，对，就是这样。所有这些我曾经梦想让助理做的事——而我的助理永远没法持续做到，因为她会分心、我们在办活动、有什么事发生了——就像拥有一个世界上最可靠的员工，每月 200 美元，24/7 工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I want to follow that thread, but first of all, what other tools do you have? Lindy's one, what else do you find really useful?
turns.zh: 好，我想顺着这条线聊，但首先，你还有什么其他工具？Lindy 是一个，还有什么你觉得特别有用？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: So the other one is Replit. So Replit is basically a vibe coding platform. You can literally go into it and say, "I want to make a website for my sound software business. Here's a big document with a bunch of details," and it'll go and design a pretty impressive website. But then you can also build web apps now. So you can literally be like, "Yeah, build a Python web app that does XYZ," and the design is getting so good because it uses Claude 4. You can start saying, "Do it in the style of Stripe. Think this through, rewrite all the copy and the tone of David Ogilvy or Malcolm Gladwell," or whoever you like, and it does a really incredible job. So what I'm finding is that things that previously would've frustrated me because I would've had to rely on a team of five, I can just do entirely on my own when it comes to web projects and stuff like that. So I'm having a blast with that.
turns.zh: 另一个是 Replit。Replit 基本上是一个 vibe coding 平台。你可以直接进去说：'我要为我的音响软件公司做一个网站，这里是一份包含很多细节的大文档'，它就会去设计一个相当令人印象深刻的网站。但你也可以构建 web 应用了。你可以直接说：'嗯，做一个做 XYZ 的 Python web 应用'，而且设计越来越好，因为它用的是 Claude 4。你可以开始说：'用 Stripe 的风格做。把这个想清楚，用 David Ogilvy 或 Malcolm Gladwell 的语气重写所有的文案'，或者任何你喜欢的人，它做得非常出色。所以我发现，以前会因为要依赖一个五人团队而让我沮丧的事情，我现在在网页项目之类的事情上完全可以自己搞定。所以我玩得非常开心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's cool. So your team Replit versus Lovable, Bolt, v0, is that roughly right?
turns.zh: 酷。你用 Replit 对比 Lovable、Bolt、v0，大致是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: I mean, they're all great. I, just am the most familiar with Replit, and it seems like it has the most functionality. It has a lot of beef to it, whereas Lovable and Bolt seem a little more basic. You might have to deal with deployment and stuff in a fiddlier way with them.
turns.zh: 我是说，它们都很好。我只是最熟悉 Replit，它看起来功能最多，内容很扎实，而 Lovable 和 Bolt 看起来更基础一点。用它们你可能得用更麻烦的方式处理部署之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. Anything else?
turns.zh: 好。还有别的吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Another one I love, so Limitless. I don't know if you've seen this.
turns.zh: 另一个我爱的，是 Limitless。不知道你见过没。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've got one of those.
turns.zh: 我有一个。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: It's really cool. So clips to your shirt. I actually just put it on my pocket so no one actually notices that I've got it on usually, and I just have it on all day. And what it does is it just records everything I do. And then I can say, the other day I had a coffee with someone and I'm the kind of person where I go a mile a minute and I say, "Oh, I'll send you that and I'll do this," or whatever. And so at the end of the day, I can just say, "Hey, what did I promise to people today?" Or even better, everyone loves this use case, I have a fight with my girlfriend. And she says, "You didn't say that." And I'm able to say, "Well, actually you did." And you can query it as an LLM. (00:50:16): So you can say you're a couples counselor. Look at this fight. What did each person need? How did it start? What are the key lines? Where did it change? How could you do this better? And so honestly, from a relationship standpoint is probably where it's been the most useful. What's cool too is that has an API. And so eventually, I haven't gotten there yet, but eventually you'll be able to just have it record your entire day and then automatically go into your Todoist or whatever it is, and add to-do's or send emails or whatever you need it to do.
turns.zh: 它很酷。夹在衬衫上。我其实就放在口袋里，所以通常没人注意到我戴着它，我就整天开着。它做的就是记录我做的一切。然后我可以说——前几天我跟人喝咖啡，我是那种一口气说一英里的人，我会说'哦，我会发给你那个，我会做这个'之类的。所以一天结束的时候，我可以说：'嘿，我今天答应了别人什么？'或者更好的，所有人都喜欢这个用例——我跟女朋友吵架了，她说'你没说过那句话'，我能说：'其实你说过。'你可以把它当 LLM 查询。(00:50:16)：你可以说'你是个情侣咨询师，看看这次吵架，每个人需要什么？怎么开始的？关键的话是哪些？哪里发生了转折？怎么做得更好？'所以说实话，从关系角度讲，这可能是它最有用的地方。很酷的是它还有 API。所以最终——我还没到那一步——最终你就能让它录下你一整天，然后自动进入你的 Todoist 之类的，添加待办或发邮件或任何你需要它做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, this is so fun. Or just per your point with the relationship, ask it, "What could I have done better today? Where did the day go downhill?"
turns.zh: 哇，这太好玩了。或者就着你那个关于关系的点，问它：'我今天哪里可以做得更好？今天什么时候开始走下坡路的？'

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Yeah, I saw a guy on Twitter. He said, "Every day I ask it, 'How could I have been a better dad?'" And it'll be like, "Oh, your daughter tried to get your attention about this. You should have paid attention," or whatever.
turns.zh: 对，我在 Twitter 上看到一个人说：'每天我都问它，我今天怎么能做一个更好的爸爸？'它会说：'哦，你女儿想引起你注意说这个事，你应该关注一下'之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that was with the Limitless data. Oh, man, I love that. With the relationship, you didn't go where I thought you were going to go, where it's like, "Oh, but who actually said it? What did you actually say?" I love that It became much more wholesome of just like how could we have communicated better holistically? Okay. My wife actually is like, "Don't wear this around."
turns.zh: 那是用 Limitless 的数据。哦，天哪，我喜欢这个。关于关系，你没去我以为你会去的方向——就是'到底是谁说的？你到底说了什么？'我很喜欢它变成了更 wholesome 的——就是我们怎么能更好地沟通？整体上。好。我老婆其实也是说：'别戴这个到处走。'

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: You just got to wear it really covertly. Honestly, I know it sounds kind of cheesy because you think like, "Oh, it'll tell her," right? But in reality, usually you're both guilty in the fight. And my girlfriend has actually appreciated it because there's been half the time it'll be like, "Oh yeah, Zoe said this and it triggered this," but a lot of the time it's me too. And I think I'm totally right. So I find it actually really helpful. Other tools, I mean otherwise, it's the basic stack of Claude and ChatGPT and Gemini. And Gemini I use mostly for things that are really large. So for example, all my medical records, I have trained on Gemini 2.5 just because the other ones can't really go through it all. Claude, I use for writing very extensively. I find it's the best for that. (00:52:14): And then ChatGPT for everything else. In terms of cool things I do, recently, I went through my entire medicine cabinet and I just took big photos that showed all the different medicines and stuff. And now I can say something like, "Hey, I'm really tired and stressed out today. What supplement should I take and what dose?" Or I'll say, "Remember all the medications I'm taking, whenever I ask you a health question, always remind me in the context of I might be taking that medication." So a few times it's said, "Hey, you shouldn't take this other medication because your genetics say you're not compatible with it and you're already taking this other one." So stuff like that's been really helpful.
turns.zh: 你就是得非常隐蔽地戴着。说实话，我知道听起来有点 cheesy，因为你会想：'哦，它会告状'，对吧？但实际上，通常吵架的时候双方都有错。我女朋友其实很感激它，因为有一半的时间它会显示'哦，对，Zoe 说了这个，然后引发了那个'，但很多时候也有我的问题。而我还觉得我完全是对的。所以我觉得它真的很有帮助。其他工具，除此之外就是 Claude、ChatGPT 和 Gemini 的基础栈。Gemini 我主要用于非常大的东西。比如，我所有的医疗记录，我都在 Gemini 2.5 上训练过，就因为其他的没法全部过一遍。Claude 我大量用于写作，我觉得它在这方面最好。(00:52:14)：然后 ChatGPT 用于其他一切。至于我做的酷事，最近我把整个药柜翻了一遍，拍了大照片显示所有不同的药和补充剂之类的。现在我可以说：'嘿，我今天很累、压力很大，我应该吃什么补充剂？什么剂量？'或者我会说：'记住我在吃的所有药，每次我问你健康问题时，总是要在我可能正在吃那种药的背景下提醒我。'有几次它说：'嘿，你不应该吃这个药，因为你的基因显示你不兼容，而且你已经在吃那个了。'所以这种东西真的很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For that use case, do you come back to a specific conversation where you've given it that context, use a project or something-
turns.zh: 对于那个用例，你是回到一个你给过它那个上下文的特定对话，还是用 project 之类的——

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: No, I say remember. I just say remember these supplements, this is what I have in my medicine cabinet or this is what I take every day.
turns.zh: 不是，我说'记住'。我就说'记住这些补充剂，这是我药柜里有的'或者'这是我每天吃的'。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see. So just tap into the memory of ChatGPT.
turns.zh: 我明白了。所以就是用 ChatGPT 的 memory 功能。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is awesome. This makes me remember that. And this connects to other points you've been making, I've started to use ChatGPT deep research to prep for these conversations. I used to have a researcher who did this for 400 bucks. They did research on every guest that I had, four to 500 bucks, and gave me a whole doc, "Here's everything about them. Here's their background, here's questions you might want to ask." Deep research is better. Just as of recently, especially with o3-pro.
turns.zh: 这太棒了。这让我想起来——也联系到你一直在说的其他点——我已经开始用 ChatGPT 的 deep research 来为这些对话做准备。我以前有个研究员，花 400 美元。他为我每个嘉宾做研究，四五百美元，给我一整份文档：'这是关于他的一切，这是他的背景，这是你可能想问的问题。'Deep research 更好。最近尤其是用 o3-pro 以后。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: We were talking earlier about agents. I forgot one of my favorite agents. So it looks on my calendar 30 minutes before I meet anyone. It goes on to Perplexity and it does a deep dive on the person and it sends me, it goes into my email and it gets the context of the meeting. So often I book meetings three months out. So I usually look at my calendar and I go, "Who is this person? I don't even remember booking this meeting." It'll text me before and it'll say, "Here's who you are, here's your background, here's the email context of why we're meeting." And it basically does all the research for me. So I do the same thing. I also use deep research and say, "If I'm meeting them, you know everything about me. What are our commonalities and what are all the fun things we should talk about?"
turns.zh: 我们之前聊过 agent。我忘了一个我最喜欢的 agent。它在我和任何人见面前 30 分钟看我的日历，上 Perplexity 对这个人做一个深度 dive，然后发给我——它进我的邮件拿到会议的上下文。我经常提前三个月订会议，所以我通常看日历然后想'这人是谁？我都不记得订了这个会了。'它会在会议前给我发消息说：'这是谁，这是他的背景，这是你们见面的邮件上下文。'它基本上帮我做完了所有研究。所以我也做同样的事，我也用 deep research 然后说：'如果我要见他，你知道关于我的一切，我们的共同点是什么？我们应该聊的所有有趣的事情是什么？'

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God, I just want to plug and play all these agents you've built to use them myself. Interestingly, I tried to create an agent to do this research kickoff for me, but I don't think you can automate ChatGPT deep research. Okay.
turns.zh: 天哪，我只想把你构建的所有这些 agent 即插即用地拿来自己用。有意思的是，我试过创建一个 agent 来为我做这种研究启动，但我觉得你没法自动化 ChatGPT 的 deep research。好吧。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Only Perplexity. Yeah.
turns.zh: 只有 Perplexity。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Perplexity is great too, but it's different. Okay. So let me follow this thread I was going down, which is around job displacement. I know you think a lot about this. So with me, this researcher as a contractor I was working with for a few months, I no longer need them. Your assistant, you no longer need. Thoughts on just the impact we're going to see on jobs as a result of AI.
turns.zh: 好。Perplexity 也很棒，但不一样。好。让我顺着我要走的这条线聊——关于岗位被取代。我知道你思考很多这个。对我来说，这个研究员——跟我合作了几个月的合同工——我不再需要他了。你的助理，你也不再需要了。关于 AI 对就业的影响，你怎么看？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: There's this great William Gibson quote, "The future is already here, it's just not evenly distributed." And I think that we are in the Palm Treo phase. Do you remember the Palm Treo?
turns.zh: William Gibson 有句很棒的话：'未来已经在这里，只是分布得不均匀。'我觉得我们正处在 Palm Treo 阶段。你记得 Palm Treo 吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不记得。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: So when I was, let's see, in 2007 I think, was that when the iPhone came out? 2007?
turns.zh: 大概是 2007 年吧？iPhone 是那一年出来的？2007？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know [inaudible 00:55:19].
turns.zh: 我知道（听不清）。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Something like that. In 2007, there was this device called the Palm Treo and it was like a little PDA with a stylus and it had a little modem attachment. And so what you could do is you could get your email anywhere and that was this shocking thing. It had a black and white or barely color screen and you could go in and email people. And I remember walking through the mall buying shoes while answering business emails and going, "This is the ultimate freedom. This is incredible." But the problem with that device was it sucked. You had to use a stylus, it's not a good user experience. And then the iPhone comes out and you're like, "Okay, this is what I was waiting for. This is the real thing." But I got a little preview with the Palm Treo and so right now people like me who have the time and skillset to nerd out and build the agents can do this. It's just not accessible to everybody. (00:56:14): And I think that if it was accessible to everybody in terms of if you could just open ChatGPT and say, "Hey, ChatGPT, I run a business, can you help me?" And it started asking you questions and it said, "Oh well you do sales. Do you want me to set up a sales agent? Okay, great, plug in your HubSpot API, now tell me a few things and then give me access to all your data." And then before you know it, it's just a digital employee that's on the other end of the phone on ChatGPT just like in the movie, Her, that you can talk to and it can go do stuff. I think that is kind of the iPhone moment that we're going to have in some time in the next five years. And so I think that if AI doesn't progress, we will see some serious job displacement, like what you already mentioned, the translators, the researchers, the admin, some assistant jobs, depending on the kind of work they do, those jobs will definitely be massively affected. (00:57:13): But I think pretty quick, all knowledge work jobs could be affected if the models scale in the way that they say they're going to. I mean if you trust Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, I mean Dario Amodei said by, "2027, our models will be smarter than all PhDs." So in any subject. That is a staggering statement. And he's been a very conservative kind of almost fearful voice in the AI world. Very cautious to say things like that. And so when he said that, I perked up and started listening carefully. I don't know that that's how it's going to play out. He might be trying to fundraise, we have to take it with a grain of salt. But if that's true, then I think so many knowledge work jobs are going to change massively.
turns.zh: 差不多吧。2007 年有一种设备叫 Palm Treo，它像一个带触控笔的小 PDA，还有一个小调制解调器附件。你能做的就是随时随地收邮件，这是件令人震惊的事。它有一个黑白或勉强彩色的屏幕，你可以进去给人发邮件。我记得我在商场一边买鞋一边回工作邮件，心想：'这是终极自由，太不可思议了。'但那设备的问题是它很烂。你得用触控笔，用户体验不好。然后 iPhone 出来了，你就觉得：'好，这才是我在等的，这才是真的东西。'但我先用 Palm Treo 得到了一个预览。所以现在，像我这样有时间和技能去 nerder out、去构建 agent 的人能做到这些。它只是对所有人来说还不普及。(00:56:14)：我觉得如果它对所有人都普及了——就是如果你能直接打开 ChatGPT 说：'嘿，ChatGPT，我经营一家公司，你能帮我吗？'它开始问你问题，然后说：'哦，你做销售，要我帮你设一个销售 agent 吗？好的，插入你的 HubSpot API，告诉我几件事，然后给我访问你所有数据的权限。'然后不知不觉，它就是一个在 ChatGPT 那头电话另一端的数字员工了，就像电影《Her》里那样，你能跟它说话，它能去办事。我觉得那大概是我们未来五年内会有的 iPhone 时刻。所以我觉得如果 AI 不继续进步，我们会看到一些严重的岗位被取代——就像你提到的——翻译、研究、行政、某些助理岗位，取决于他们做哪种工作，这些岗位肯定会大受影响。(00:57:13)：但我觉得很快，所有知识工作岗位都可能受影响——如果模型按照他们说的规模扩张的话。我的意思是，如果你信 Sam Altman 和 Dario Amodei——Dario Amodei 说'到 2027 年，我们的模型会比所有博士都聪明'，在任何学科。这是一个惊人的声明。而且他在 AI 世界里一直是非常保守、几乎是恐惧的声音，非常谨慎说这种话。所以当他说那个的时候，我竖起耳朵开始仔细听。我不知道会不会那样发展，他可能在融资，我们要打折扣听。但如果那是真的，那我觉得非常多知识工作岗位会发生巨变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, there's a lot here. I actually had Mike on the podcast, their CPL, Mike Krieger, and he pointed out that Dario, every prediction he's had so far has been right over the past few years. And so there's a reason to listen to his insights. Okay. Andrew, I know you're not going to have all the answers for people. But let me ask you kind of a two-part question for new grads and for people currently in the workforce say like, I don't know, senior product manager advice on what they should do, where should they focus? What skills will matter most? What jobs do you think will last? What advice can you give us?
turns.zh: 好，这里有很多内容。我其实请过 Mike 上播客——他们的 CPO Mike Krieger——他指出 Dario 到目前为止过去几年的每个预测都是对的。所以有理由听他的洞察。好。Andrew，我知道你不会给所有人答案。但让我问你一个两部分的问题——对于新毕业生和对于已经在职场的人，比如资深产品经理——关于他们应该做什么、应该聚焦哪里？什么技能最重要？什么工作会留下来？你能给我们什么建议？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Everybody 10 years ago, do you remember there was this whole movement that we should teach kids how to code? Remember that?
turns.zh: 10 年前每个人——你记得有一阵子整个运动是教孩子学编程吗？记得吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mh-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Now teaching kids how to code is teaching kids Basic and we have a GUI, right? You don't need to learn punch cards and basic programming or MS-DOS because we all have keyboards and mice. We don't have to do that. And I feel like coding has really gone away because of that. And I think now people are saying people need to learn how to prompt, which I think is very true for the tool set right now. But I don't know how relevant that is in the future because I think we're still, again, in the Palm Treo phase, I think that the AIs will be very good at eliciting what the actual problem you're trying to solve is and reinterpreting it in a way that it can optimize the query to get the right answer and solve the problem. (00:59:38): And so I think the fundamental question is do all jobs just become a single prompt? For example, does a CEO just grow the business while making the customers happy and turning a profit or something like that? And it is able to actually be an omniscient presence that can run a whole company. Now that's a big I'm someone building AI agents. I can barely get it to reliably do calendar entries and that kind of stuff. So I don't think that's totally imminent, but I can certainly see a world where that's coming. And so the question is, what is one to do when that reality is barreling down at you?
