For people who have resources, I think there's a lot of things they can do in terms of investment, they can invest in the companies that'll benefit from this, companies that have a lot of compute or energy or that sort of thing. (01:00:29): So that's one thing, but that's not really the question. The question is what do you do if you're a smart 18-year-old or 19-year-old or whatever? In my opinion, I think the best thing to do right now is to get incredibly good with these tools and utilize them to build enough wealth that you can put the money into diversifying into compute and energy. And I do think that while everybody thinks that all jobs will go away in five years and robots will be everywhere, people generally overestimate things in the short term and underestimate them in the long term. So I think there's going to be this long window where robotics is not anywhere near good enough to even do raking leaves and stuff. And I think there's going to be a ton of opportunity for people to just spin up new businesses that never existed before. (01:01:20): I was talking to some friends and we were like, "What do you do in a world of abundance where everything is really cheap and companies operate almost autonomously?" I think there's a lot of weird skillsets that we can't imagine right now. For example, just being funny, right? Being funny to hang out with them. Think about OnlyFans, right? Right now, there's this whole idea of OnlyFans where people are paying for comfort and connection, but in a romantic sense. Imagine people did that day to day, they just love hanging out with funny people. So you have a funny guy who you chat with or comes over to your house or whatever it is, I'm making stuff up. Maybe it's a guy who comes to play pickleball with you or something, I don't know. But I can imagine that in this weird world, there's all these weird new jobs. (01:02:06): So I think my take is things will either be totally fine or they will be terrible and we'll all be dead. And I can't predict which those is there. I don't think it's worth thinking about all of us being dead. And so I think it's really just lean into what are the tools, how do you stay cutting edge? How do you build businesses and wealth in this new world? But I am certainly feeling a little bit like all of our brains could be defunct in the next 10 years. And that's kind of a scary thought.
turns.zh: 现在教孩子学编程就像教孩子 Basic 而我们已经有 GUI 了，对吧？你不需要学打孔卡和基础编程或 MS-DOS，因为我们都有键盘和鼠标，不需要那个了。我觉得编程真的因为这样而消失了。我觉得现在人们在说人需要学怎么 prompt，我觉得对现在的工具集来说这很对。但我不知道未来这还相不相关，因为我觉得我们仍然——再说一遍——在 Palm Treo 阶段。我觉得 AI 会非常擅长引导出你真正想解决的是什么问题，然后用一种它能优化查询以得到正确答案、解决问题的方式来重新解读它。(00:59:38)：所以我觉得最根本的问题是：所有工作是不是都变成一句 prompt？比如，CEO 是不是只要增长业务、让客户满意、赚钱之类的？然后它能真的成为一个全知全能的存在来运营一整家公司。那是个很大的——我是一个构建 AI agent 的人，我勉强能让它可靠地做日历条目那种事。所以我不觉得那完全迫在眉睫，但我当然能看到那个世界正在到来。所以问题是，当那个现实朝你冲来的时候，你该怎么办？对于有资源的人，我觉得他们可以做很多投资方面的事——投资于会从中受益的公司、有很多算力或能源的公司之类的。(01:00:29)：那是一方面，但那其实不是问题。问题是如果你是一个聪明的 18 岁、19 岁的人，你怎么办？在我看来，我觉得现在最好的事情就是变得极其擅长这些工具，并用它们建立起足够的财富，然后你可以把钱多元化到算力和能源上。我确实觉得，虽然所有人都觉得五年内所有工作都会消失、到处都是机器人——人们通常高估短期、低估长期。所以我觉得会有一个很长的窗口期，机器人技术远远不够好，连耙叶子都做不好。我觉得会有大量机会让人去做以前从来没有过的新生意。(01:01:20)：我跟一些朋友聊，我们就想：'在一个一切都变得很便宜、公司几乎自动运营的丰饶世界里，你做什么？'我觉得有很多我们现在想象不到的奇怪技能。比如，仅仅是搞笑，对吧？搞笑到能跟他们待在一起。想想 OnlyFans，对吧？现在 OnlyFans 是人们为舒适和连接付费，但是是浪漫意义上的。想象一下人们日常也这么做——他们就爱跟搞笑的人待在一起。所以你有一个搞笑的人跟你聊天或者来你家之类的——我在瞎编——也许是一个来跟你打匹克球的人，我不知道。但我能想象在那个奇怪的世界里，有这些奇怪的新工作。(01:02:06)：所以我觉得我的看法是：要么一切都没事，要么会很糟糕，我们都会死。我预测不了是哪个。我不觉得值得我们都会死这件事值得想。所以我觉得真的就是——拥抱这些工具是什么，你怎么保持前沿？你怎么在新世界里建生意和财富？但我当然有点觉得我们所有的脑子可能在十年内就没用了。这是个可怕的想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm picturing this dystopian world where humans are just going around making jokes.
turns.zh: 我在想象这个反乌托邦的世界，人类就到处去讲笑话。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Where does status come from in a world of abundance? Where does status come from? Maybe it is just like being the best at hiking or something.
turns.zh: 在一个丰饶的世界里，地位从哪来？地位从哪来？也许就是做最好的徒步者之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, let me ask you this because this is where it gets even more real is just with your kids. What are you encouraging them to learn? What are you encouraging them to get good at? Because this is the real problem a lot of people are having right now is what will matter in the future. Obviously we don't know, but what are you encouraging them to focus on?
turns.zh: 好，让我问你这个，因为这里变得更真实了——就是你的孩子。你鼓励他们学什么？你鼓励他们擅长什么？因为这是很多人现在面临的真实问题——未来什么会重要。显然我们不知道，但你鼓励他们聚焦什么？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Well, I don't know. I mean there's so little, they're five and eight. And so really what I'm focused on is making sure they're socialized and they're polite, very basic. So are they comfortable talking to adults? I often send my son, whenever he wants something at a cafe, I always make him go up, ask nicely, pay himself, all that kind of stuff. But at this point I feel like for the first 10 years of life, you're just trying to make sure that they're not traumatized or rude. And I think it's going to be really interesting when they're 10 plus where they're really aware of this stuff and can start building with these tools. And to be honest, I just don't know. I think I just want them to lean into whatever they're passionate about and go from there. But I have no idea. And to be honest, it's not something I'm worrying about because it's too hard to worry about. I don't know, it's too multivariate. There's too many ways it can go.
turns.zh: 嗯，我不知道。他们才五岁和八岁，太少 了。所以我真正关注的是确保他们社交化、有礼貌，非常基础的东西。他们跟大人说话自在吗？我经常让我儿子——他每次在咖啡馆想要什么，我都让他自己去问、礼貌地问、自己付钱之类的。但在这一点上我觉得人生前 10 年你只是想确保他们没有创伤、不粗鲁。我觉得当他们 10 岁以后，真正意识到这些东西、能开始用这些工具构建的时候，会很有趣。说实话，我就是不知道。我想让他们投入到他们热爱的事情里，然后从那里开始。但我真不知道。说实话，这不是我担心的事，因为太难担心了。我不知道，变量太多了，有太多走向了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like a core part of your message is just get good with these tools. There's this classic quote, "AI won't replace you, it'll be somebody very good using AI is going to replace you," at least for a while. And so it feels like a big part of this is just use these things. Before we started recording, we were having a mic issue and I love you just went straight to ChatGPT, "ChatGPT, how do I connect this mic to reverse side and make it work?" And I feel like that's just a habit to build is just like go to ChatGPT whenever you have a problem like that. I've been doing that a lot. I was connecting a subwoofer from what wire do I need to buy to connect the subwoofer to the receiver?
turns.zh: 我觉得你的核心信息的一部分就是——擅长这些工具。有句经典的话：'AI 不会取代你，会用 AI 的人会取代你'——至少在一段时间内。所以感觉这里很大一部分就是用这些东西。我们开始录音之前，麦克风出了问题，我喜欢你直接去问 ChatGPT：'ChatGPT，我怎么把这个麦克风连到反面让它工作？'我觉得那就是一个要建立的习惯——就是有问题就问 ChatGPT。我也一直在这么做。我接一个低音炮，需要买什么线把低音炮连到接收器？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Well, the best part about ChatGPT is I used to just get stuck and I have ADHD. So when I got stuck, let's say, what's an example? I was redoing my home IT security. And what will happen is I'll be in the terminal and I'll enter something and then something goes wrong and it just keeps erroring. And then I'm like, "Well, I'm out." I have ADHD, I can't tolerate this. I just lose the thread completely. And ChatGPT allows me to stay on track and go so much further and faster than I ever could before. I love not being artificially stopped in your tracks and being able to continue the flow state as a result.
turns.zh: 嗯，ChatGPT 最好的一点是我以前就是会卡住，我有 ADHD。所以当我卡住——举个例子——我在重做家里的 IT 安全。会发生的就是我在终端里输入东西，然后出错了，然后一直报错。然后我就'好吧，我不行了'。我有 ADHD，我受不了这个，我完全失去线索了。ChatGPT 让我能保持在轨道上，走得比我以前能走的远得多、快得多。我喜欢不被人为地停下来，能继续心流状态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And also I noticed you were using voice mode, which is what I've been using more and more. And I feel like that's something a lot of people sleep on is just the voice mode where you could talk to it and not have to sit there and type your questions. Okay, so let me go in a different direction. You've been spending a lot of time, you wrote a whole book about this, of just your journey from, you call it Barista to Billionaire where you started serving coffee, then you ended up being very successful, then realize that didn't make you happy. You're quite unhappy with lots and lots of money. I think a lot of people hear these stories, they see this stuff, they're like, "Yeah, okay, I sort of get it." But they still do the same sorts of things. They still assume they will be happy once they reach that next goal, that next title, make certain dollar amount. What can you share? What have you learned about just what it actually takes to be happy that you think people are still not really recognizing and still kind of are confused about?
turns.zh: 而且我注意到你在用 voice mode，我也越来越多地在用。我觉得很多人忽略了它——就是 voice mode，你可以跟它说话，不用坐在那里打字。好，让我换个方向。你花了很多时间，写了一整本关于这个的书——你从咖啡师到亿万富翁的旅程，你从端咖啡开始，然后非常成功，然后意识到那没让你快乐。你有很多钱的时候很不快乐。我觉得很多人听到这些故事、看到这些东西，会想'嗯，好吧，我大概懂了'。但他们还是做同样的事情。他们还是以为一旦达到下一个目标、下一个头衔、赚到某个金额就会快乐。你能分享什么？关于到底怎样才能快乐，你觉得人们还是没真正认识到、还是困惑的？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Do you remember when you're in your early 20s? I remember when I was in my early 20s, I'd always be like, "I need to move away to Europe. I need to go discover myself." And I'd be really anxious and stressed out and in an existential crisis and then I'd fly to Europe to go backpacking or something and I'd still feel anxious and have my existential crisis. It's just now I'm in Europe. And I think the reality is that whatever's in your brain, whatever that anxiety loop is, doesn't go away just because you have a bigger house or more money in the bank account or you're in Bali or wherever it is, that's a chemical reaction happening inside you that relates to your past and your DNA and all that stuff that creates that soup. And for me, I've always been a very anxious person. I've always worried about tomorrow, I rarely enjoy today, I'm always worrying about what could go wrong in health or my businesses or with my family or whatever it is. (01:07:12): And so when I started my business, all I thought was I just don't want to work for someone else. If I can just wake up in the morning, do my own thing, make 60K a year, then I'll be happy. So I got that and then it was once I make a million dollars a year and I can buy a house, well, I got that and so on and so on and so on all the way up to at one point being worth over a billion dollars, by the way, should redo the title of the book from Barista to Billionaire, now it's former billionaire because our stock went down, but it didn't change anything. I'm still just as anxious as ever. I remember a month ago, I had this day where I was sitting in the sauna and I was stressing about a bunch of business problems and money things and I stopped myself and I was like, "Wait a minute." (01:08:04): 10 years ago I had all the same thoughts and I was stressed out about similar kinds of problems and our revenue was $20 million bucks or $15 million bucks. Now we're at almost 300 million and I'm still stressed about the same things. And the saddest part was as I met more and more wealthier people all the way up to multibillionaires, I realized they were all still comparing themselves to their peers, competing over who has what and tracking stuff and still unhappy that anxiety loop or depression was still in their brain. I remember I had this moment where I met this guy who is a single-digit multibillionaire, and he goes, "Oh, Jeff Bezos, he's just so fucking rich." And I was like, "Wait, what do you mean you're worth $5 billion? What can he do that you can't?" And he goes, "He can buy a super yacht." And it's like, "What?" (01:09:09): You can look at that guy and you can say, "Oh, that's a wacko and all the other stuff." But the reality is that we're all just comparing ourselves to our peers, whatever our peers have that we don't feel hard done by. And I remember just thinking like, "Oh my God, how do I avoid becoming this?" And that's the scary reality is no matter how lucky you are, I mean we're also fortunate. For me, I live in Canada. I have every opportunity that I ever could have hoped for. And there's people all over the world who have nowhere near what I had growing up. And yet I felt hard done by because in my neighborhood I was the poor kid. I wasn't poor globally. I wasn't even poor based on Canada. But all my friends had big screen TVs and would go to Hawaii and I never got to do any of that stuff. My parents were stressed about money. So I feel hard done by.
turns.zh: 你记得你 20 岁出头的时候吗？我记得我 20 岁出头的时候总想着：'我得搬去欧洲，我得去发现自己。'我会很焦虑、很压抑、处于存在主义危机中，然后我飞去欧洲背包旅行之类的，我还是焦虑、还是存在主义危机，只不过现在在欧洲。我觉得现实是，你脑子里的东西、那个焦虑循环，不会因为你有了更大的房子或银行里更多的钱或你在巴厘岛就消失——那是你体内发生的化学反应，跟你的过去和 DNA 等等所有东西有关，形成了那锅汤。对我来说，我一直是个非常焦虑的人。我总是担心明天，很少享受今天，总是在担心健康或生意或家人可能出什么问题。(01:07:12)：所以我开始创业的时候，我满脑子想的只是我不想给别人打工。如果我能早上醒来、做自己的事、一年赚 6 万，那我就会快乐。然后我得到了那个，然后就是一旦我一年赚 100 万就能买房子，好，得到了，然后如此循环，一路到某个时刻身价超过 10 亿美元——顺便说一下，应该把书名从《从咖啡师到亿万富翁》改成《前亿万富翁》，因为我们股票跌了——但这没改变任何东西。我还是一样焦虑。我记得一个月前，有一天我坐在桑拿房里，为一堆生意问题和钱的事焦虑，然后我停下来想：'等等。'(01:08:04)：10 年前我有完全一样的想法，我为类似的问题焦虑，那时我们的收入是 2000 万或 1500 万。现在我们接近 3 亿了，我还是为同样的事情焦虑。而最悲哀的部分是，当我遇到越来越多更富有的人，一路到身家几十亿的亿万富翁，我意识到他们都还在跟同龄人比较，比谁有什么、追踪这些东西，还是不快乐——那个焦虑循环或抑郁还在脑子里。我记得我有这样一个时刻，我遇到一个身家几十亿的人，他说：'哦，Jeff Bezos，他真他妈有钱。'我就想：'等等，你什么意思，你身价 50 亿美元？他能做什么你做不了的？'他说：'他能买一艘超级游艇。'就这？(01:09:09)：你可以看那个人然后说：'哦，那是个疯子'之类的。但现实是我们都在跟自己的同龄人比较，无论我们的同龄人有什么我们没有的，我们就觉得委屈。我记得当时就想：'天哪，我怎么避免变成这样？'而可怕的现实是，不管你多幸运——我们也很幸运，对我来说，我住在加拿大，我拥有我曾经能希望的一切机会。世界上到处都有的人成长条件远不如我。但我觉得委屈，因为在我的社区里我是穷孩子。按全球标准我不穷，按加拿大标准我甚至不穷。但我的朋友们都有大屏电视、都去夏威夷，我从来做不了那些。我父母为钱焦虑。所以我觉得委屈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a phrase of friend's financial advisor once shared, "The Joneses are doing really well," and that's hard to get over. So what changes did you make to just be happier? It's hard to give up money. It's hard to give up more money you could make. It's hard to give up things that money buys, I guess just so what did you change?
turns.zh: 有个朋友的投资顾问说过一句话：'隔壁的 Jones 家过得可真好'——这很难克服。那你做了什么改变让自己更快乐？放弃钱很难，放弃能赚到的更多的钱很难，放弃钱能买到的东西也很难——所以你改变了什么？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Well, there's a few things. I mean, one was reframing money to some degree to have it be something that wasn't just about feathering my own nest and making it better. So for example, I was talking to a friend who's very wealthy and I was saying all the feelings I described of have all this and yet I don't feel better. And he said, "Well, what are you working for?" And I said, "Well, I guess I'm just working for the numbers to get bigger and have more employees and that's nice. Our businesses do good things in the world and help more people and stuff, but ultimately it's just to pile up cash." And he said, "I've reframed it so that all my money, 90% of my money plus, goes into my philanthropic foundation and then it gets given away to great causes. So when I think about working really hard or losing a deal or an investment going well, the win isn't for me. The win is about doing something good." (01:11:26): So I did that and that definitely helped. I also stopped spending as much money. I found that the more stuff I had, the more houses I had, the more people that directly worked for me to manage all that stuff, the less happy, I was owned by my stuff. And then I work really hard not to have people... I try not to beat people over the head with it. I drive a normal car. I don't bring people to my house until I know them really, really well. I meet them on neutral ground, I meet them in a cafe. I dress like a schmo. I just try not to be a weird out of touch rich person. But the biggest thing, which is a weird answer, is actually medicating myself. So basically all my life I've been really anxious. (01:12:18): And in 2020, I remember I was watching a movie with my ex-wife and I was looping on, "I need to respond to this email. If I don't respond to that email, this person's going to be mad." And then I realized that I was watching a movie for the last 20 minutes and I didn't know anything about what was happening in the movie. And then I was going, "Oh my God, my wife is going to be mad at me. We're going to get in a fight," and I'm projecting all this negative stuff. And in that moment I was like, "Okay, maybe I do need to try an SSRI or something. This is not sustainable." And so I went to my doctor and I got prescribed with one, and I remember I was so scared of it that I cut it into 10 pieces. I said, "I'm just going to take a tiny little piece." (01:13:01): And it took me six months after that to try any. But I started taking these pieces every day and I just noticed that within about three or four days, it was like someone had turned down the volume on the nasty voice inside of me doing all that. And for the first time in my life I felt relief. No amount of money or success or attention or anything else had done what this little tiny yellow pill could do for my mental state. And so now I've been on an SSRI for four and a half years or something like that. And then I also started medicating my ADHD. And I would say that my brain went from Times Square to a quiet library. And I think a lot of people are scared of that, but ultimately most people are acting out something that's going on inside of them. There's a trauma or something medically going on and that's creating this anxiety, this depression, this feeling and addressing that is so much more important than trying to get praise from the external world.
turns.zh: 嗯，有几件事。一个是重新定义金钱，让它不只是为了给自己捞好处。比如我跟一个很富有的朋友聊天，我说我描述的所有那些感觉——有这一切但不觉得好。他说：'那你为什么工作？'我说：'嗯，我猜就是为了让数字变大、有更多员工，挺好的。我们的生意在世界上做好事、帮到更多人之类的，但归根结底就是堆钱。'他说：'我重新定义了，让我所有的钱——90% 以上——进入我的慈善基金会，然后分给好的事业。所以当我想到拼命工作或者一笔投资做得好不好，赢的不是我，赢是做了一件好事。'(01:11:26)：所以我那样做了，那确实有帮助。我也减少了花钱。我发现东西越多、房子越多，直接为我工作来管这些东西的人越多，我越不快乐——我被我的东西拥有了。然后我很努力不让人……我尽量不拿这个砸人。我开一辆普通的车。我不带人来我家，直到我非常非常了解他们。我在中立地带见他们，在咖啡馆见。我穿得像个 schmo。我就是尽量不做一个古怪、脱节的富人。但最大的事情——这是个奇怪的答案——其实是给自己用药。基本上我一辈子都很焦虑。(01:12:18)：2020 年，我记得我跟前妻看电影，我在循环：'我得回这封邮件，如果我不回，这个人会生气。'然后我意识到过去 20 分钟我在看电影，但我完全不知道电影在演什么。然后我在想：'哦天哪，我老婆要生我气了，我们要吵架了'，我在投射所有这些负面的东西。那一刻我想：'好吧，也许我真的需要试试 SSRI 之类的了。这不可持续。'于是我去看医生，开了一种，我记得我太害怕了，把它切成 10 片。我说：'我就吃一小片。'(01:13:01)：之后我花了六个月才敢试。但我开始每天吃这些小片，我发现在三四天内，就像有人把我脑子里那个 nasty 的声音的音量调低了。我这辈子第一次感到解脱。没有任何金额的钱、成功、关注或其他任何东西能做到这片小小的黄色药丸为我的精神状态做到的事。所以现在我用 SSRI 大概四年半了。然后我也开始用药治我的 ADHD。我会说我的脑子从时代广场变成了一个安静的图书馆。我觉得很多人害怕这个，但归根结底大多数人是在表演某种内在发生的事情——有一个创伤或者某种医学上的问题在制造这种焦虑、抑郁、这种感觉——处理那个比试图从外部世界获得赞美重要得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, it's really powerful. I really am really thankful you're sharing this. The advice most people hear, the general, I don't know, culture is just like, "No, don't take meds. Don't medicate yourself, I don't know, there's all these downsides, all this risk. The pharma industry is trying to make money." I love this other perspective of it. It's actually really effective and actually makes a big difference in your life and it may be the only solution.
turns.zh: 哇，这真的很强大。我真的很感谢你分享这个。大多数人听到的建议、普遍的文化是：'不，别吃药，别给自己用药，有各种坏处、各种风险，制药行业想赚钱。'我喜欢这另一个视角——它其实很有效，真的能在你的生活里带来很大的改变，可能是唯一的解决方案。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Well, it's funny because if you have a headache, I don't think many people say, "Oh, don't take Tylenol, you're benefiting Johnson & Johnson, big pharma." They go, "Yeah, you take a Tylenol when you have a headache." Or a lot of people have seasonal allergies and they take antihistamines and they forget that histamine is not just in your nose, histamines in your brain and everywhere in your body. And so when you take an antihistamine or even a Tylenol, you're changing your brain, you're changing the way you think, you're changing everything. And yet for some reason, people are so scared, myself included, of taking an SSRI or similar medication to treat something that is ruining their life. Anxiety was ruining my life. Every minute of every day I was convinced that something terrible was about to happen. And even now medicated, I still have that voice. It's not like that frankly beneficial voice that helps you grow your business or whatever becomes unproductive at a certain point. And I think that it is wonderful to be able to actually just get a little bit of solace from it.
turns.zh: 嗯，有趣的是如果你头痛，我不觉得很多人会说：'哦，别吃 Tylenol，你在让强生、大制药赚钱。'他们会说：'对啊，头痛就吃 Tylenol。'或者很多人有季节性过敏，吃抗组胺药，他们忘了组胺不只在你鼻子里，组胺在你大脑和身体各处。所以当你吃抗组胺药甚至 Tylenol 的时候，你在改变你的大脑，改变你思考的方式，改变一切。但不知道为什么，人们——包括我自己——如此害怕吃 SSRI 或类似的药来治疗正在毁掉他们生活的东西。焦虑在毁掉我的生活。每时每刻我都相信可怕的事情即将发生。即使现在用药了，我还是有那个声音。那个声音——坦白说那种有益的、帮你增长业务的声音——在某个时刻变得不生产性。我觉得能够从它那里得到一点点慰藉真是太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, for folks that, I mentioned many folks listening, are like, "Oh man, I should really explore this," what's the best way to explore is to talk to your primary care physician?
turns.zh: 对于那些——我说了很多听众会想'哦，我真的应该探索一下'——最好的探索方式是什么？是跟你的初级保健医生谈吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Yeah. I think talking to your doctor, and one note I think a lot of people miss is when I was so scared of side effects because you hear about all these horrific side effects of people lose their libido and feel terrible and stuff. And so I looked into it and a lot of the side effects are due to the way that people metabolize different drugs. And so you can actually do your 23andMe or similar DNA test and you can find out how you metabolize different SSRIs. And then I chose one that I could metabolize well. And so I've had no side effects or problems. And I know every time I mention this, I get a lot of people that say exactly what you say, big pharma and all this other stuff. But I just ask everyone listening, if you take a Tylenol or you take an antihistamine or other medications, I don't know why something that can be so profoundly helpful is something that people need to be afraid of.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得跟你的医生谈，有一个 note 我觉得很多人忽略的是——我之前太害怕副作用了，因为你听到各种可怕的副作用——有人失去性欲、感觉糟糕之类的。所以我研究了，很多副作用是由于人们代谢不同药物的方式不同。所以你可以去做 23andMe 或类似的 DNA 测试，你能知道你如何代谢不同的 SSRI。然后我选了一种我能很好地代谢的。所以我没 有副作用或问题。我知道每次我提这个，会有很多人说你说那些话——大制药之类的。但我就是请每个听众想，如果你吃 Tylenol 或吃抗组胺药或其他药，我不知道为什么能如此深刻地有帮助的东西是人们需要害怕的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Andrew, we've covered so much ground. I love the spectrum of topics we've gone after. Is there anything else that you wanted to share? Anything you wanted to double down on? Any last nugget you want to leave listeners with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 太棒了。Andrew，我们聊了特别多。我喜欢我们涉及的话题范围。还有什么你想分享的？有什么想强调的？在我们进入非常精彩的快问快答之前，有什么最后想留给听众的金句吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: One thing that was shocking for me was I was doing... My doctor asked me to get a cognitive test, not because I had any problem, but he said, "Look, it's really important to get a baseline in your 30s because then as you age, we can make sure that you're not getting Alzheimer's or dementia or whatever." So I go and I do this test with a neurologist and she asked me a bunch of questions. It's, "Remember these 10 digits and say them backwards and all this stuff." And finally when I get my test results back, she said, "Look, your crystallized intelligence, your ability to remember stuff, long range is totally fine. You're above average. Your short-term memory, your working memory is 10th percentile, very, very bad. And you probably should get checked for ADHD." (01:17:47): And I was like, "Nope. There's no way. I don't have ADHD. I'm organized. I've got to-do lists. I built a business. I wasn't the hyper kid in school or anything like that." And she said, "Well, look, just humor me. Just go get tested." And so I went through this crazy process. You can go online and just quickly get tested or whatever. But I went through this really, really five-day process to get tested. And it turned out that I do have it. And it's really interesting because if you take the normal population of about 5% of people have ADHD, but about 30% of entrepreneurs have ADHD. And many entrepreneurs I talk to, they love new things. They love jumping around between a million different topics. They're an inch deep and a mile wide like I described. And they describe themselves as unemployable. And frankly, I remember I was so skeptical of ADHD that when my girlfriend told me, a friend of hers got diagnosed with it, I sarcastically said, "Oh good, she better take some meth," talking about stimulant drugs. (01:18:54): Previously I was very, very skeptical of ADHD, but it is a real brain disorder if you actually dig into it. It's a very real thing, very objective that people have poor executive function. And for me, it's given me a lot more empathy for myself and my behaviors because at work, if you have ADHD, you can delegate to other people and build systems to get around your disability. But at home, that's where it really plays out. And so for me, it's like my girlfriend asked me to take the garbage out, and I say, "Of course." And then I forget three times in a row. And she views that as you are being very hurtful and you're not caring for me. And it causes all sorts of different problems at home. (01:19:37): And so for me, not only did it make my work life better because I was more focused, but it actually really helped me in my personal life and it made me feel not broken. I always felt a bit broken. I couldn't put my finger on why, but I just went, "I'm not good at doing all the things everyone else seems to be able to do no problem." And so I think especially because you have an entrepreneur audience, I think a lot of entrepreneurs should consider getting checked for ADHD. Just go and ChatGPT say, "Ask me a of questions and tell me if you think I might have it." But I was very surprised, and that's been really impactful for me too.
turns.zh: 一件让我震惊的事是——我医生让我做一个认知测试，不是因为我有什么问题，而是他说：'看，在 30 多岁的时候建立一个基线很重要，这样随着你年龄增长，我们可以确保你没有得阿尔茨海默或痴呆之类的。'所以我去跟一个神经科医生做了这个测试。她问我一堆问题，就是'记住这 10 个数字然后倒着说出来'之类的。最后我拿到测试结果，她说：'看，你的晶体智力——你记忆东西的能力、长程的——完全没问题，你高于平均。你的短期记忆、工作记忆是第 10 百分位，非常非常差。你大概应该查一下 ADHD。'(01:17:47)：我说：'不，不可能。我没有 ADHD。我有条理，我有待办清单，我建了公司，我在学校不是那个多动的孩子之类的。'她说：'嗯，看，就当陪我，去测一下。'于是我经历了这个疯狂的过程。你可以上网快速测一下之类的，但我经历了一个非常非常五天的过程来测。结果是我确实有。这很有意思，因为普通人里大概 5% 有 ADHD，但创业者里大概 30% 有 ADHD。我聊过的很多创业者，他们都爱新东西，爱在一百万个话题之间跳来跳去，像我描述的那样一英里宽一英寸深。他们形容自己'无法被雇佣'。坦白说，我记得我之前对 ADHD 太怀疑了，当我女朋友告诉我她的一个朋友被诊断出 ADHD 时，我讽刺地说：'哦好，她最好吃点冰毒'——说的是兴奋剂药物。(01:18:54)：以前我非常非常怀疑 ADHD，但如果你真的深入研究，它是一种真实的大脑障碍。它是非常真实的东西，非常客观——人们的执行功能差。对我来说，它给了我对自己和自己行为的很多同理心，因为工作时如果你有 ADHD，你可以委托给别人、建系统来绕过你的障碍。但在家里，那才是它真正表现出来的地方。对我来说，就是我女朋友让我倒垃圾，我说'当然'，然后我连续忘三次。她把这看作你在伤害我、你不关心我。在家里引起各种不同的问题。(01:19:37)：所以对我来说，它不仅让我的工作生活更好因为我更专注了，它还在我的个人生活里真的帮了我，让我不觉得自己坏掉了。我一直觉得自己有点坏，我没法指出为什么，但我就是觉得'我不擅长做所有人似乎都能轻松做到的事'。所以我觉得——特别是因为你的听众是创业者——我觉得很多创业者应该考虑查一下 ADHD。就去 ChatGPT 说：'问我一堆问题，告诉我你觉得我有没有。'但我非常惊讶，这对我也很有影响。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Man, this garbage story is very descriptive of my life, and so I'm going to do this. There's this implication that it's good to know this, right? It feels scary to feel like, "Oh, shit I might get diagnosed with ADHD." Your advice I imagine is it's better to know because you could do stuff about it.
turns.zh: 天哪，你这个 garbage story 很生动地描述了我的生活，所以我要去做这个。这里有个暗示是知道这个是好的，对吧？感觉害怕——'哦，糟了，我可能被诊断出 ADHD'。我猜你的建议是知道更好，因为你能做点什么。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Totally. I think it's like any medical thing, right? It's like there's an Alzheimer's gene, right? And if you know you have it, there's a lot you can do to slow the disease or prevent maybe getting it or whatever. It's always better to know. Even if you don't medicate, I think there's a lot of lifestyle interventions, dietary interventions, and just things you can do to make your life easier, even if it's just explaining to your partner, "Hey, I need things to be explained to me this way so that I can be effective in loving you."
turns.zh: 完全。我觉得这跟任何医学的事一样，对吧？就像有阿尔茨海默基因，如果你知道你有，你可以做很多事来减缓疾病或也许预防得病之类的。总是知道更好。即使你不用药，我觉得有很多生活方式干预、饮食干预、你能做的事让生活更轻松——哪怕只是跟你的伴侣解释：'嘿，我需要用这种方式被解释事情，这样我才能有效地爱你。'

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Beautiful. Okay. Well, Andrew, with that, we've reached a very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太好了。好，Andrew，那我们就到了非常精彩的快问快答环节。我有五个问题给你。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Let's go.
turns.zh: 来吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题：有哪两三本书是你发现自己最常推荐给别人的？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: If I could only recommend two, I would recommend The Laws of Human Nature by Robert Greene. It's basically like a compendium of every single type of personality disorder or psychological effect. How do people work their minds to make bad decisions? What is a narcissist? What is a psychopath? All that kind of stuff. And Robert Greene does such a great job of telling all that in a really engaging way by using storytelling. So every single chapter has a story about someone with that personality disorder. So I love that book. (01:21:48): The other one that I love is a book by Felix Dennis called How to Get Rich. It's hilarious because the whole book starts out saying, "I got rich and I regret it, and I wish that I'd become a poet." And instead he went off and he built this huge publishing empire, became a poet in his sixties, and then he died of throat cancer. So it's his story, he basically says, "I'll tell you how to build the business even though you probably shouldn't." And I read that when I was in my 20s, and I found it so exciting and inspiring, and then I recently reread it and I was like, "Oh my God, why didn't I listen to this guy?" Everything he said came true.
turns.zh: 如果只能推荐两本，我会推荐 Robert Greene 的《The Laws of Human Nature》。它基本上是每一种人格障碍或心理效应的合集。人们是怎么让自己的心智做出糟糕决定的？什么是自恋狂？什么是 psychopath？所有这类东西。Robert Greene 做得非常好，用讲故事的方式把所有这些讲得非常引人入胜。每一章都有一个关于某种人格障碍的人的故事。所以我爱那本书。(01:21:48)：另一本我爱的 是 Felix Dennis 写的《How to Get Rich》。它很搞笑，因为整本书一开始就说：'我发财了，我后悔了，我希望我当初做个诗人。'结果他出去建了这个庞大的出版帝国，60 多岁成了诗人，然后死于喉癌。所以这是他的故事，他基本上说：'我来告诉你怎么做生意，虽然你大概不应该。'我 20 多岁的时候读到这本，觉得非常激动、非常受启发，然后我最近重读了一遍，心想：'天哪，我为什么不听这家伙的？'他说的一切都应验了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Next question, do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show that you have really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 下一个问题：你最近有没有一部最喜欢的电影或电视剧，你真的很享受？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: I love Challengers. I don't know if you've seen it, but it's amazingly acted, amazing cinematography. It's like this amazing romantic triad tennis movie. Really, really good.
turns.zh: 我喜欢《Challengers》。不知道你看过没，但演技惊人、摄影惊人。它就像一部浪漫三角关系网球电影。真的非常好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite product you recently discovered that you really love? You already mentioned Limitless. Is there anything else?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有发现一个你很爱的最爱产品？你已经提过 Limitless 了。还有别的吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: I'm one of those people who really believes in the idea of a robot vacuum. I've probably spent $10,000 on different robot vacuums over the years, probably five or six of them. And I finally got one that actually works. It's called the Matic Vacuum, M-A-T-I-C. And basically, I think it's like former Google Engineers basically built like a mini Waymo car. So it has machine vision and it will avoid absolutely everything and never get tangled, and it can mop your floors and vacuum. I've been super impressed with it so far.
turns.zh: 我是那种真的相信机器人吸尘器的人。这些 年我大概在各种机器人吸尘器上花了一万美元，大概五六个。我终于找到一个真的能用的。叫 Matic Vacuum，M-A-T-I-C。基本上我觉得是前 Google 工程师做了一个像迷你 Waymo 汽车的东西。它有机器视觉，会避开所有东西、永远不被缠住，还能拖地和吸尘。我目前非常 impressed。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've got one of these myself. Completely agree. My wife loves it, which I did not expect. She's like, "Turn that Matic on." It's very delightful. It has his little personality and it just does a really good job. And I'm not an investor, and that's awesome. I'm a huge fan. Okay, next question. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to find useful in work or in life?
turns.zh: 我自己也有一个。完全同意。我老婆也很爱它，这我没料到。她说：'把那个 Matic 开起来。'它很讨喜，有点小个性，做得非常好。我不是投资人，这太棒了。我是超级粉丝。好，下一个问题。你有没有一个最喜欢的座右铭，经常回来、在工作或生活中觉得有用？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Yeah. My favorite is a quote by Jerzy Gregorek. It's, "Easy choices, hard life. Hard choices, easy life." And I often find that anytime that I'm making the easy choice, my life gets hard. And when I make the hard choice to shut down the business, fire the person, say bye to a project that I was excited about, it's almost always the right choice and it makes my life a lot easier.
turns.zh: 有。我最喜欢的是 Jerzy Gregorek 的一句话：'简单的选择，艰难的人生。艰难的选择，简单的人生。'我经常发现任何时候我做了简单的选择，我的人生就变难。当我做了艰难的选择——关掉公司、开除那个人、跟我曾经兴奋的项目说再见——几乎总是对的选择，让我的人生轻松很多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. Okay, so let me know if this is true. I found that when you were a teenager, when you're running Macteens, you interviewed Steve Jobs at a conference. Is that true?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。好，让我知道这是不是真的。我发现你十几岁、运营 Macteens 的时候，在一个会议上采访过 Steve Jobs。是真的吗？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: So when I was a teenager, I had a tech news website and I emailed the Apple PR people and I said, "Hey, could I interview Steve Jobs?" And they kind of laughed at me. They're like, "Yeah, there's no way. You're not going to interview Steve Jobs, but hey, why don't you go to this tour of the Apple Store?" So this is no other Apple Store has existed. This is in New York at Macworld back in 2004, no, 2003, something like that. And so I was really excited about that. So I show up to go do this tour and there's 30 other journalists there, and I'm first in line, and this big black SUV pulls up and this man gets out and the man is wearing gray New Balance, little circular John Lennon glasses, the mock turtleneck. And my brain finally puts it together and I realize it's Steve Jobs. (01:25:11): And he walks directly up to me because I'm first in line and he shakes my hand and he says, "Hi, I'm Steve." And I'm like a quivering mess. I'm 17 years old. He is my hero. He's my Jesus. And so I was just so high on adrenaline that I just started asking him questions. As soon as we walked in, I basically just stayed at his side, and I just picked his brain about all sorts of different stuff. So it's not like I got to ask him questions about life. I was asking him about the new 17-inch iMac or whatever. But it was a pretty cool experience to get to meet him.
turns.zh: 我十几岁的时候有一个科技新闻网站，我给 Apple 的 PR 发邮件说：'嘿，我能采访 Steve Jobs 吗？'他们有点笑我，说：'嗯，不可能。你采访不到 Steve Jobs，但嘿，你要不要去参加这个 Apple Store 的参观？'这是在没有任何其他 Apple Store 存在之前，是 2004 年还是 2003 年在纽约 Macworld 上。我非常兴奋。于是我去做这个参观，那里有 30 个其他记者，我排在第一个。一辆黑色大 SUV 开过来，一个男人下车，穿着灰色 New Balance、小小的圆形 John Lennon 眼镜、mock turtleneck。我的脑子终于拼出来了——那是 Steve Jobs。(01:25:11)：他直接走向我，因为我排第一。他跟我握手说：'嗨，我是 Steve。'我抖得不行，我 17 岁，他是我的英雄、我的耶稣。我肾上腺素飙到天上，直接开始问他问题。我们一走进去，我基本上就一直在他身边，就各种各样的事问他。所以不是我采访他关于人生的问题，我问他的是新的 17 寸 iMac 之类的。但能见到他是一次相当酷的经历。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is awesome. There's such a funny thread recently with guests. Everyone, there's like a Steve Jobs connection for the past couple months of guests. That's an awesome story. It just shows that it wasn't luck. You made this happen. You got there first in line.
turns.zh: 这太棒了。最近有个很好笑的线索——各位，过去几个月的嘉宾每个人好像都有 Steve Jobs 的关联。这是个很棒的故事。它说明那不是运气，是你让这件事发生的。你排到了第一个。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: The lesson for me was ask big and maybe you'll get something great. Ask for amazing, you'll get something great, which I did.
turns.zh: 对我来说，教训就是——往大了要，也许你能得到很棒的东西。要惊人的东西，你会得到很棒的东西——我就得到了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes, door in the face technique, I think people call it.
turns.zh: 对，door in the face 技术，人们这么叫它。

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Andrew, this was incredible. Two final questions. Where can folks find you if they want to reach out? I know you're buying companies, investing in companies. Just talk about what you're looking for there in case people are like, "Oh, this is me." And then finally, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: Andrew，这太棒了。最后两个问题。如果大家想联系你，能在哪里找到你？我知道你在买公司、投公司。简单讲讲你在找什么样的，以防有人说'哦，这是我'。最后，听众怎么能帮到你？

turns.speaker: Andrew Wilkinson
turns.en: Yeah, my business is Tiny, T-I-N-Y.com, and we buy businesses. Basically, when we sold the business, we hated it. We went through this process where we talked to all these douchebags that ran private equity firms that would show up in our office in suits and use a bunch of words we didn't understand. And we ended up going, "Man, why can't we just sell to somebody who's like us?" And so we basically started Tiny to become the buyer we wish we could have sold to.
